The Instagram statement begins: "We got this wrong. We've completed a full review and confirmed that Suno Studio was used to regenerate the original track. We shared inaccurate information, and we're truly sorry."

Until then, the company had denied using AI, even releasing a video showing DAW stem files. YouTubers were the ones who dug into that claim. Danny Sapko raised the first questions, and scrutiny spread around a heavily processed progressive metal performance demo. Rhett Shull obtained the stem files directly and looked further into the controversy.
D'Addario artists like Yvette Young and Mike Dawes initially defended the brand. Things escalated after the company deleted critical comments and one employee claimed to have been doxxed.

In the statement, D'Addario said it had also mishandled comment moderation. "Honest criticism should not be erased." It added that it would change how it runs its channels so people are protected from threats, harassment, and doxxing while still being heard.

It also laid out a new policy. "We do not support AI-generated music, and our process will reflect that going forward." Employees and creative partners will now be required to disclose whether generative AI was used in content, and the company will review that disclosure closely.

It closed by saying it knows one statement won't fix this, that D'Addario exists because musicians have entrusted their sound to its products, and that it will earn the same trust in how it treats this community.

blocks.cap: Noizefield Audio Plugin Coder

blocks.x: Music software maker Noizefield has released Audio Plugin Coder (APC) 1.4.0, a major update to the open-source framework that uses AI coding agents to turn plugin ideas written in natural language into VST3/AU project structures.

APC guides users through ideation, architecture design, UI design, implementation, testing, and packaging, while carrying forward project state and troubleshooting knowledge throughout. It's aimed at producers, sound designers, and developers who don't want to start from an empty C++ project. It runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux alongside agents like Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Kilo, and Antigravity.

Here's what's new in 1.4.0. It upgrades from JUCE 8 to JUCE 9.0.1, picking up support for the latest hosts, tooling, and WebView-based UI. /apc-setup is a first-run wizard that checks the toolchain and sets plugin, build, and release folder locations, UI defaults, and per-step AI model preferences.

Workflow commands also got unique names, like /apc-dream, /apc-plan, /apc-design, /apc-impl, and /apc-ship — a change meant to avoid name collisions with other AI tools, though short aliases like /dream still remain. Dependency checking has gotten tighter, and the WebView plugin documentation has improved. Build scripts were fixed to recognize paths correctly, and WebView UI smoke tests on Windows were verified against actual plugin builds.
APC 1.4.0 is available for free on GitHub, with the source code open as well.

blocks.cap: The transparency provision of the EU AI Act, in force since August 2

blocks.x: Since August 2, new transparency provisions under the European Union's AI Act have taken effect. Audio, images, video and text that AI created or substantially altered must now clearly disclose that they are “artificial”.
Developers of general-purpose AI systems now face new transparency obligations as well. It marks the first milestone consumers can actually feel in the EU's flagship AI legislation.
For the music industry, the change isn't about blocking AI but about making its use visible. It doesn't ban AI music, nor does it settle the copyright disputes over AI training data.

Instead, “the focus is on transparency”. Content that AI created or substantially altered must be recognizable to listeners, and developers must document how they trained their models and meet the AI Act's transparency requirements.

The music industry's biggest legal questions remain unanswered. The new rules don't determine whether companies like Suno or Udio infringed copyright by training on copyrighted recordings, nor do they require disclosing every song used in training. That fight continues in courtrooms and licensing negotiations around the world.
What Europe has set is a single baseline: “AI-made content can no longer be anonymous”.

For artists, labels and rights holders, it becomes easier to identify AI-generated output and examine how it is presented to listeners. Holding companies accountable for how they used AI also gets easier. Companies that violate the transparency requirements can face fines of up to €15 million, or 3% of their annual global revenue.

blocks.cap: The Spotify and Kobalt logos on a black background

blocks.x: Spotify has been teasing an AI tool that lets fans make covers and remixes for a while now. It has already disclosed a partnership with Universal Music Group. The new partner is indie music publisher Kobalt, a company that publishes songs for a wide range of musicians, from Phoebe Bridgers to post-punk band IDLES.

Kobalt artists will soon be able to opt into Spotify's new platform, where fans take songs and rework them into remixes and covers, powered, of course, by a suite of AI tools. No one has heard the results yet. Think something like Suno, but using only properly licensed songs instead of scraping the whole internet.

So the tool is being promoted not as a new way for generative AI to rip off artists, but as a new way for them to make money. Spotify says it will “open up additional revenue streams and new ways to drive discovery”. Kobalt CEO Laurent Hubert added that its artists are “directly benefiting from the creative opportunities these new features provide”.

At least it's clear where that revenue will come from. The platform will launch as a paid add-on for Premium subscribers. It's still unknown how much it will cost, or whether anyone will actually pay to make an AI cover of a favorite song.

It's also unclear whether there will be a way to make covers without AI. If it really all comes down to licensing, what's the difference between algorithmic slop and a real cover performed and recorded by a human? Either way, answers will take a while to arrive. Spotify hasn't said when the tool will launch.

blocks.cap: Suno co-founder and CEO Mikey Shulman. Photo by Samuel Boivin / Shutterstock

blocks.x: Suno has added another badge to its collection. The AI music platform and BMG jointly announced a new deal on August 12. BMG's press release described it as a “global alliance that establishes a strategic framework covering BMG's recorded and music publishing repertoire”, a strategic framework spanning its recorded music and publishing catalog.

The press release notes the opt-in element for BMG artists. “The agreement ensures that BMG artists and songwriters who choose to participate have their rights protected and are compensated for their music, while also settling prior use of BMG recordings and publishing works.” Artists and songwriters who choose to participate have their rights protected and get compensated, and past use is settled as part of this deal.

BMG is the first major rights holder to sign a licensing deal with Suno since Warner Music Group partnered with the company nine months ago. The largest rights holders, Universal Music Group and Sony Music Group, are still suing Suno in the United States, alleging widespread copyright infringement in training its earlier models.

Suno co-founder and CEO Mikey Shulman said, “We believe the future of music will be more participatory, creating entirely new ways for artists and fans to connect.” He added that building that future responsibly means working directly with the people who make the music.

blocks.cap: Celine Joshua, EVP of Global Marketing and Streaming at BMG

blocks.x: Celine Joshua, BMG's EVP of Global Marketing and Streaming, made clear that choice is the guiding principle. “This agreement establishes strong protections, clear economics, and new creative possibilities for artists and their fans.” Protections are strong, the economics are clear, and the creative possibilities are new.

The BMG announcement came the same week Suno confirmed it would cap how many downloads subscribers can make. The cap, which takes effect next month, is meant to “make it harder for bad actors to mass-export music”. Suno also plans to add audio watermarking and fingerprinting technology.

In June, Suno raised more than $400 million at a $5.4 billion valuation and passed 100 million users. Last month, it lost a dispute with Germany's GEMA in the Munich Regional Court, which ordered it to disclose revenue information and pay damages. BMG holds more than 3 million songs and recordings, including catalogs from will.i.am, Jean-Michel Jarre, Tina Turner and Paul Simon. Its scale will grow further with a multibillion-dollar merger with Concord set to close in the fourth quarter.

blocks.cap: Uppbeat Creator Report 2026

blocks.x: AI has surged into the creator economy, reshaping the digital landscape. Content has exploded, and authenticity has come under pressure. Instead of forecasting the future, creative asset platform Uppbeat asked creators directly.

The newly released Uppbeat Creator Report 2026 is based on a survey of 1,792 creative professionals and 13 in-depth interviews conducted between February and March 2026. It examines how creators, including musicians and YouTubers, are adapting to new technology, which AI tools they embrace, and which parts of the creative process they refuse to hand over to machines.

The line is clear. “Just 6.7% of respondents finding fully AI-generated content acceptable”, meaning only 6.7% of respondents accept output that is entirely AI-made. Yet “60% are happy to integrate AI assistance” into their workflow. Contrary to tech-industry assumptions, “16- to 24-year-olds are the least likely group to use AI tools”, using them the least of any age group.

blocks.cap: Where artists draw the line on AI — Uppbeat Creator Report

blocks.x: Three themes emerged from more than 2,600 open-ended responses. Specificity matters more than volume. As AI makes mass production easier, “creators are standing out by getting more specific and niche” rather than simply increasing output. Audiences are pushing back too, quietly scrolling past overly automated, predictable content in favor of something “messy, emotional, and brilliant”. And amid an endless supply of AI-generated material, the one scarce resource left is a creator's individual perspective and voice.

There's advice for independent musicians too: hand off chores like metadata, promo scheduling, email drafts, clip editing and work logistics to AI, but keep songwriting, recording vocals and meeting fans in person for yourself. Mass-producing predictable tracks just gets swallowed by the algorithmic sludge. What turns people into paying fans is an extremely specific aesthetic and a vulnerable, personal story.

Hypebot's conclusion is this: there's no need to fear AI, nor to hand over one's entire creative identity to it. Use the tools to strip away backend friction and buy back time, then spend that time on raw, direct connection, through songs, shows and the merch table. In an age of endless synthetic noise, a personal story is a competitive edge that goes beyond branding.

AI should be an exciting technology. In a short time, it has produced a flood of new tools, techniques, sounds and ways of working. Yet a handful of the biggest AI companies have turned that promise sour: algorithms that swallowed human-made music whole are regurgitating it.

Fortunately, some companies put music and musicians first. The ethical AI described here means brands that build their tools together with musicians, producers and artists. Instead of “make my record sound like XYZ artist,” they license material directly from collaborators. Above all, they don't use your music to improve their products.

blocks.cap: In front, LANDR Layers; behind, LANDR Blueprint. Image: LANDR

blocks.x: LANDR. Mastering was AI's canary in the coal mine. It has sold algorithmic mastering since 2014, refining its algorithms by learning directly from engineers who agreed to it. Even with competition tightening, it still offers the best balance of price, flexibility and quality. Its one flaw is that online mastering comes bundled with distribution services, so anyone who doesn't want that has to buy the standalone plugin separately.

blocks.cap: Project LYDIA, made together by Roland and Neutone. Image: Press

blocks.x: Neutone. It staked out ethical AI from the start, using only self-recorded data or datasets pulled from the public domain. Morpho, built on that data, transforms the timbre of a real-time input according to the character of the AI model. That means you can pull drums out of a voice or drive a Gregorian chant with a guitar riff. It splits 50% of model revenue with artists. One model was trained using only a human heartbeat. Each model's training method and sources can be checked directly inside the plugin. Project LYDIA, built with Roland to put AI into a physical stompbox, is also underway.

blocks.cap: The Voice-Swap VST plugin. Image: Voice-Swap

blocks.x: Voice-Swap. AI voice cloning had a bad reputation early on, and for good reason. From the start, Voice-Swap partnered directly with singers to build artist-approved voice models that can be used legally in commercial music. Fifty percent of subscription fees go straight to the participating artists. Setting ethics aside, its cloning technology ranks among the best in the industry, and it also offers VST plugins and custom voice model creation.

ACE Studio. It bets everything on a workstation that's AI from head to toe. Its AI features range from generating accompaniment to producing an entire song from a single sketch. The review found text-to-music wasn't quite there yet, but the AI vocal models were different. Because participating musicians were paid, it was possible to dig through 140 vocal models with a clear conscience. They were surprisingly realistic, and you could blend and layer them to build your own timbre.

blocks.cap: Moises AI's Stem Generator. Image: Moises AI

blocks.x: Moises AI. Stem separation draws almost the only complaint-free reception in the AI debate. Splitting finished recordings into pieces changed the game for DJs, remixers and audio restoration workers. Moises AI partners with musicians, labels and platforms and licenses all of its training data. This year, Charlie Puth joined as chief music officer, standing alongside Jordan Rudess and Cory Henry.

Safari Audio Meaw Chain. It's the most interesting AI music plugin released this year. Play audio in your DAW for Meaw Chain to analyze, write a direction in text, and a plugin chain comes out in seconds. Safari has said it will never train on customer audio. Its list of supported third-party plugins keeps growing, and it even catches individual parameters inside them. Being a first release, it has plenty of rough edges, but ethics isn't one of them.

blocks.cap: Alibaba's AI songwriting model HappyShrimp 1.0, now in beta

blocks.x: Alibaba has released an AI model that turns a single written prompt into a finished song. The Hangzhou-based company said HappyShrimp 1.0 entered beta on Monday, August 17.
HappyShrimp works with the Chinese label group Taihe Music Group on co-creation with artists and content development. Taihe Rye Music and Ocean Butterflies belong to the group.

When a user writes a mood, a story or a music style, HappyShrimp writes the melody, arrangement and lyrics and performs the vocals itself. Users can also supply their own lyrics for the model to set to music, or ask for an instrumental track alone. The company says no musical training is required.

The genres it covers include Chinese-style music, pop, R&B/soul, hip-hop, rock, funk, electronic, classical and jazz. Prompts can specify instrumentation, vocal style and how the energy shifts as a song unfolds. Before generating sound, it first lays out the song's structure, rhythmic development and chord progression, alongside emotional tone, energy and lyrical intent.

The model comes from Alibaba Token Hub, the AI organization Alibaba set up in March 2026 under group CEO Eddie Wu. It follows the multimodal model HappyHorse and the world model HappyOyster, both released earlier this year.

One of the world's largest tech companies has entered a market where Suno and Udio hold the name recognition. Suno raised more than $400 million in June at a $5.4 billion valuation and says it has surpassed 100 million users. Both companies came to the negotiating table after the RIAA sued on behalf of the three major labels in 2024 over “mass infringement.”

Inside China, the field is already crowded. Kunlun Tech runs the Mureka generator and Melodio streaming service, and ByteDance has its own mobile music-creation tool. Tencent Music Entertainment's Tianqin Lab built a music model with Tencent AI Lab and added DeepSeek to its creation tool, letting songs publish straight to QQ Music.

Alibaba owns every layer beneath the model itself, from chips to cloud to frontier-grade AI systems. Its largest model, Qwen3.8-Max, released August 3, has 2.4 trillion parameters. The company has positioned it as a frontier system just behind Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.

This isn't Alibaba's first move into music. It bought the streaming service Xiami Music in 2013 and shut it down in February 2021. Last July, Damai International, the overseas arm of its entertainment division, launched the artist-development label ORCA and held auditions worldwide. According to the IFPI, China grew 20.1% in 2025, overtaking Germany to become the world's fourth-largest recorded music market.
Apple Music told partners. Music that is “substantively generated” on AI platforms like Suno will get a 'Made With AI' label by the end of this year.
That's only if labels and distributors have already attached the relevant metadata before the track reaches the platform.

This was laid out in a message Apple sent to industry partners on Thursday, August 20, which MBW obtained. A tagging system that Apple Music has been running behind the scenes since March will now become visible to listeners too. Apple calls these tags AI Transparency Tags.

With these tags, labels and distributors have been marking whether AI was used in the track, composition, artwork, and music video individually. Until now, these were only visible inside Apple's content delivery feed.

“We ask that labels and distributors tag content as such when they submit content that is substantively generated by AI,” Apple wrote in the memo that day. “Later this year, we will make this tag visible to Apple Music users in the form of a Made With AI label.”

Content providers “should include AI Transparency Tags in all cases where AI was used to create a substantive part of the content, including tracks generated by AI platforms,” Apple added. “AI platform generated content refers to anything derived primarily from a generative AI service.”

Here, the “obligation” sits with the supply chain, not the platform. Apple Music doesn't detect AI content itself to apply the label; it relies on labels and distributors to report it. That's the same approach it took when it introduced the tags in March.

This self-reporting approach contrasts with news Spotify put out earlier this month. On August 11, Spotify announced it would add an “AI Persona” badge to artist profiles that present an AI-generated identity. For that badge, it said it “won't rely solely on self-reporting,” and will directly review and flag profiles whose public identity “appears to be a realistic AI-generated identity.”

However, Spotify's badge points to the artist, not the music. On the music side, it relies on self-reported credits, just like Apple's label. Deezer uses its own technology to catch and clearly mark tracks it suspects were AI-made.

There's regulatory context too. The EU AI Act's transparency rules, which took effect August 2, require generative AI system providers to embed machine-readable markers in their output. Services already on the market before that must meet this requirement by December 2, and Suno is among them.

Suno said on August 6 that it would introduce audio watermarking and fingerprinting “within weeks,” working with distribution platforms to “address fraud and misuse.” If a marker is embedded at the point of generation, it becomes easier to identify AI tracks downstream, and labels and distributors gain a technical means to verify before tagging content on Apple Music or other DSPs.
The RIAA and IFPI announced an industry-wide push last July to get AI-made tracks clearly labeled across major streaming services worldwide.

blocks.cap: SSG Audio Loudness Pro

blocks.x: SSG Audio has released Loudness Pro. Instead of using a fixed threshold, it's a mastering limiter that recalculates its clipping and limiting parameters thousands of times per second. There's only one knob, and an AI engine manages the balance between the clipper and the limiter at sample-level resolution.

Typical limiters require an engineer to set the threshold, ceiling, release, and amount of clipping by hand. Loudness Pro continuously re-balances the clip-to-limit ratio in real time. The goal is to reduce the pumping and crushed transients that come from a fixed value drifting out of sync with a changing source, while keeping loudness consistent.

It also includes Auto Dither Control (ADC), which applies dither automatically only when needed for a 16-bit export, with no need to switch it on or off by hand. Latency at 48kHz is about 5ms, so it doesn't have to stay limited to offline processing — it can be left on during a mastering session with real-time monitoring.

SSG Audio positions Loudness Pro as a tool to place at the very end of the mastering chain, after tone and dynamics work are done. Single-purpose loudness maximizers already exist in plenty, but this one sets itself apart by having AI manage the parameters behind a simple interface.

The company is a collaboration between the development teams at Nuro Audio and Exonic UK, and it targets mastering engineers and producers who want competitive loudness without having to maintain a complex multi-stage limiter chain.
It runs as AU, VST2, VST3, and AAX 64-bit on macOS 10.13 and later and Windows 10/11. The list price is $150, and it's available now at a launch price of $74.

blocks.cap: OpenTune, a free open-source AI pitch correction tool for vocals

blocks.x: OpenTune is a free, open-source pitch correction tool that runs on Windows and macOS.

It's still in beta, but it's worth a look if you're after a free alternative to Melodyne or Auto-Tune, and the AI-based approach adds to that. For a potential user like me, the biggest hurdle is that the interface is in Chinese.

This is pretty much what we do at BPB: poke around at plugins that look sketchy on your behalf. We gave this one our best shot too, but since we don't currently have a Windows machine, we only tested the macOS version, on our main laptop.

The macOS installer is pretty heavy for a plugin — around 780MB — and it isn't signed, so you have to bypass macOS's security warning to install it. After installation, Studio One didn't show the VST3; only the standalone version opened.

So this test is only half complete. At the very least, we confirmed the standalone version works. If bypassing security warnings or dealing with a foreign-language interface puts you off, we'd suggest skipping this one.
Still, for anyone curious, here's what OpenTune is.

Rather than relying solely on traditional DSP pitch shifting, OpenTune runs RMVPE pitch extraction and a PC-NSF HiFiGAN neural vocoder on top of ONNX Runtime. The developer says the goal is to reconstruct vocals with corrected or shifted pitch while preserving the original formants.
In other words, it's meant to avoid the “duck voice” effect, or the sound of someone else's voice entirely, that can show up when pitch correction is pushed hard. That's their claim, at least.

The workflow openly takes cues from manual pitch correction software like Melodyne. It includes hand-drawing, note editing, anchor tools, automatic key detection and auto-tuning. It also supports correction scales such as Chromatic, Major, Minor, Pentatonic, Dorian, Mixolydian and Harmonic Minor.
OpenTune V1.5 Beta added a VST3 ARA2 extension. In compatible hosts like Studio One or Logic Pro, this should let you use region binding and rendering, but it never loaded in my copy of Studio One.

The latest beta adds Undo/Redo with up to 500 steps, a floating render-status badge, reduced memory use, improved note generation and official macOS support. GPU acceleration runs through DirectML on Windows and CoreML on macOS.
It can import WAV, FLAC, OGG and MP3, and the interface supports Chinese, English, Japanese, Russian and Spanish. The GitHub page and most of the demo material are in Chinese.
The macOS release isn't fully notarized, so that's a judgment call for each user — it means trusting your antivirus and OS-level security tools.
It's licensed under AGPL v3.0. It comes as a standalone app and a VST3 plugin, and ARA2 is also available in compatible hosts.

blocks.cap: The infringement claims include James Brown's I Got You (I Feel Good). Photo: Hulton Archive/Getty

blocks.x: Round Hill Music has filed copyright infringement lawsuits against Suno and Anthropic. It made clear it has no intention of settling either case. The complaints were filed August 17 in the Northern District of California.

Each suit seeks statutory damages of up to $150,000 for each willfully infringed work. Round Hill believes the total for each suit could reach “hundreds of millions of dollars and potentially approach or conceivably exceed $1 billion.”

The plaintiffs are Round Hill Music LP and five affiliated funds and holding companies. Between them, they hold 14,364 songs and 16,873 recordings. The complaint attaches 500 songs as representative examples for now, with plans to expand to more than 10,000. The songs at issue include Goo Goo Dolls' Iris, Jim Steinman and Bonnie Tyler's Total Eclipse of the Heart, and James Brown's I Got You (I Feel Good). Combined, the three have been streamed more than 6 billion times.

The Suno suit also names the Israeli data-scraping company Bright Data Ltd. and its U.S. subsidiary as defendants. The claim is that they supplied proxy networks and scraping tools that let Suno harvest music from licensing platforms.

Round Hill founder and CEO Josh Gruss said: “We are not against artificial intelligence. We are against the idea that you can build a business worth billions on top of other people's creative work and pay the creators nothing.” He also said he intends to pursue accountability through trial.
Round Hill brought in Richard S. Busch, the lawyer who won the “Blurred Lines” case on behalf of Marvin Gaye's estate. Both complaints demand a jury trial.

Anthropic is already defending three music copyright suits in the same court. Concord Music Group, Universal Music Publishing Group and ABKCO filed one in October 2023 over roughly 500 songs, and the same publishers filed another in January 2026 covering more than 20,000 songs while seeking more than $3 billion.

Suno's situation is complicated too. The three major labels, led by the RIAA, sued in Boston in June 2024, and Universal and Sony remain plaintiffs. On July 31, the Munich Regional Court, ruling in a case brought by GEMA, found Suno had no right to use the association's repertoire and ordered it to disclose revenue and pay damages.
Founded in 2010, Round Hill runs a $1.1 billion portfolio and 200,000 copyrights with a team of just over 50 people. It has not yet announced any AI licensing deals.

blocks.cap: AI music detection by SubmitHub (Photo: cottonbro studio)

blocks.x: Nearly 40% of music released worldwide last month showed signs that AI was involved somewhere in the production process, according to a new SubmitHub study.
SubmitHub's AI music detector analyzed more than 1 million tracks released in July, and 23.2% of them were entirely AI-generated.

On top of that, another 15.3% of songs showed signs of AI-generated audio that had been “edited or processed” by a human. That puts nearly 40% of July's releases as having been made with some involvement from AI.
SubmitHub is a platform that lets artists submit music to playlists and blogs. When it unveiled its AI detection tool, SH Labs, in June, it said it wanted to address a “growing disclosure problem.”

“We think the path forward for AI music is disclosure,” said SubmitHub founder Jason Grishkoff. “People should be able to decide for themselves whether they want to engage with AI-made music. Our job is to give them enough information to make that choice.”

The data SubmitHub has gathered includes this: among artists whose music was flagged as involving AI at the time of this year's release, 31% told the platform, when asked, that they hadn't used any AI tools at all.

The detection tool is currently used by Bandcamp and Traxsource. It's also used by GEMA, the rights management organization that recently won a landmark ruling in a lawsuit against the AI music generation platform Suno.
That July ruling found that Suno had no right to use music managed by GEMA to train its AI models, and that it had violated both German and U.S. copyright law.

blocks.cap: I AM CHOIR

blocks.x: AM I AUDIO has released I AM CHOIR, a choir instrument that takes a sung vocal and turns it into a choir part that follows the same lyrics, melody, phrasing, and timing.
It's not a common vocal doubler, and it's not a choir pad library either. It's a tone-transfer tool that reshapes an input performance into the sound of a recorded choir.

It runs locally inside the DAW. There's no cloud processing, and audio never leaves the computer. Licensing is perpetual too, so there's no separate subscription, tokens, or generation credits to buy.

There are three choir models. Gospel Choir is a mixed choir conducted by Erica Howard, with a range from E2 to G5. Kids Choir is a bright children's choir recorded with the MUSYCA Children's Choir, with a range from G#2 to G5. Shout is a male gang vocal model for shouted, non-melodic parts, with a range from E2 to G5.

AM I AUDIO says it worked directly with the singers behind the models. The singers took part knowing what the work was and consenting to it, were paid for the recording sessions, and will share in royalties if the plugin does well.
There are also several microphone models. The U67 and C12/C24 are attached to every choir, Schoeps goes with Gospel and Shout, and Telefunken goes with Kids.

On the arrangement side, there's an octave generator, plus a harmony generator that creates thirds and fifths above and below the lead, with key and scale settings attached. There's also a stereo/mono toggle.

Post-processing is limited to low cut, brightness, and reverb amount. AM I AUDIO recommends feeding in dry vocals and trimming long silences before conversion. It also advises layering octaves above and below to make the choir sound bigger.
Engineering and design were done together with Neutone, Inc.

Pricing is a launch price of $169 through September 1, rising to $199 after that. A 14-day free trial is available with no credit card. It supports VST3, AU, and AAX on macOS 12 and above; Windows isn't ready yet, so only a beta program is open.

blocks.cap: LALAL.AI Lynx

blocks.x: Few ingredients bring a track to life like a vocal sample. Whether it's an a cappella, a stem, or a single line from an old movie, one voice changes the grain of a song. The problem is that clean sources are hard to come by. YouTube videos vary wildly in audio quality, and records are hard to use once the noise gets bad.

LALAL.AI, known for its stem separator, has released Lynx, a new algorithm that strips noise and artifacts out of vocals. According to the company's blog, it was trained for a year to separate the grime of the sound from the human voice. It's available on the web, in the desktop app, and in the iOS app for iPhone and iPad, and it also attaches as a DAW plugin at the Pro tier.

blocks.cap: Voice & Noise settings

blocks.x: Using it is simple. Drop a file into the app, choose Voice & Noise, and it goes into the cleanup mode that contains Lynx. The neural network stays set to v7 Lynx, and you pick a noise-removal intensity among Mild, Normal, and Aggressive. Attack Magazine wrote that Normal struck the best balance between cleanup and preserving sound quality. For sources recorded in a room with heavy reverb, you also turn on the de-echo option.

The first test bed was dialogue from an old horror film whose copyright had lapsed. Running the scratchy original through Normal made it usable, and after cleaning it up, time-stretching it, and adding EQ and compression, it went into a speed garage track laid over a Splice loop.

blocks.cap: A cappella vinyl experiment

blocks.x: The second test was a cappella vinyl. We ripped the vocal version of Fingers Inc and Chuck Roberts' “My House” from YouTube at 240p, then deliberately layered on scratches, pops, and electrical noise in Ableton Live using iZotope's free Vinyl plugin. Aggressive removed the noise well but also shaved away the source material itself, so we dropped to Normal, and the original's slapback echo called for de-echo as well. It isn't perfect, but it's far better than before.
Lynx doesn't erase noise — it separates it. So you also get back a file containing whatever got pulled out.

blocks.cap: Kiss live vocal stem

blocks.x: The last test imitated a remix job. We picked a live recording layered with crowd cheers: Kiss's “Do You Love Me?” from the 1970s, a track on the upcoming live album Kiss Destroys Anaheim 76. Pulling the stem with Vocal & Instrumental wasn't as clean as hoped, because of the applause and shouting. We ran Normal and de-echo on it once more and laid it over an acid house track built on a Splice loop.
LALAL.AI Lynx is split into a free Starter tier, Lite at $7.5 a month, and Pro at $15 a month. One-time top-ups are also available.

blocks.cap: StemDeck

blocks.x: Solo developer Thales Pereira has released StemDeck, a free, open-source stem-separation tool that runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
The reason behind it is modest. He wanted to get his kid practicing drums, and needed a way to pull stems without paying for a subscription or uploading music to someone else's server.

He had used tools like Ultimate Vocal Remover and Go-Splitter before, but StemDeck is notably free of extras. It's free, runs locally, is open source, and requires no account, quota, upload, or subscription.

Separation is handled by the open-source Demucs model htdemucs_6s. It splits into up to six parts: vocals, drums, bass, guitar, piano, and everything else. The device is chosen automatically — CUDA on NVIDIA, MPS on Apple Silicon, or CPU otherwise.

It can import common formats like MP3, WAV, FLAC, OGG/Opus, MP4, and M4A, and you can paste in a YouTube link if you have the rights to process that content. The GitHub page is explicit, though, that StemDeck is not a downloader, and that copyright and platform terms are the user's responsibility.

Once separation finishes, a browser-based multitrack mixer opens. You can mute, solo, and balance tracks, monitor a single stem, zoom into the waveform, and loop sections. You can export stems individually or bundle them into whatever mix you want.
If you pick only some stems, the rest get collected into a separate 'Original' lane. That's useful for A/B comparisons or for practice.

Song analysis is built in too, with BPM detection, key and scale estimation with confidence, integrated LUFS, and sample peak. MP4 export is also available, so if you worked from an MP4 or YouTube source, you can lay your current mix back onto the original video.

The local network option is an interesting touch. According to the developer, opening StemDeck to the same network in settings lets your computer handle the processing while the library and mixer get operated from another device.

It's still alpha. It's enough for practice, remix prep, transcription, sampling groundwork, and experimentation, but it isn't meant to be a drop-in replacement for a polished commercial service. On first run it downloads a Python runtime, FFmpeg, and the Demucs model, and it launches much faster after that. Windows offers a choice between CPU-only and NVIDIA CUDA builds, and macOS splits into Apple Silicon and Intel downloads.
StemDeck is up on GitHub and has already passed 2,000 stars. The developer said downloads topped 13,000 in a little over two months — almost entirely by word of mouth.

blocks.cap: Train your own AI

blocks.x: For the past few years, musicians have been asking the wrong question about artificial intelligence. Can AI write a song? Of course it can. It can write compositions, mimic voices, produce orchestral cues, and turn out techno, ambient, country, film scores, and something jazz-adjacent. Let's stop pretending to be surprised.

The more interesting question comes next. What happens when a musician stops asking a giant AI for generic music and starts building a system centered on themselves instead — not an AI trained on all music, but an AI trained on their music. Recordings and performances, voice, MIDI, scores, demos, stems, improvisations, discarded ideas, mistakes, production decisions, even notes.

Some people have already done this. YACHT ran its own catalog through machine learning while making Chain Tripping and used the results as composition material. Instead of the album becoming history the moment it was finished, it became terrain you could walk into from a different direction.

Actress created a computational alter ego called Young Paint, and Holly Herndon treated Spawn like a member of her ensemble. She later released Holly+, a synthetic version of her own singing voice. Grimes opened up an AI version of her voice for other creators to use. That's the point where the model itself becomes an artist's asset.

Imogen Heap's Mogen goes beyond sound. Carrying interviews, notes, and production decisions, it leans toward knowing why something was made rather than just what was made. Reinier Zonneveld's R² responds to his playing onstage and generates MIDI to drive synths and drum machines directly. That was only possible because he kept thousands of hours of archive instead of discarding it.

This technology is now becoming a feature. Suno has added custom models that build a personal model from relatively little self-recorded material, and open-source fine-tuning is within reach on an ordinary computer. The question has shifted from “how do I build a model” to “which folder do I hand over.”

The author warns against letting the first command be “write my next album.” That, he says, is surrender dressed up as efficiency. Instead, he suggests things like: show me ten harmonic solutions I wouldn't normally pick. Push a song that stalled in 2003 in five different directions. Find the gesture I've been repeating without realizing it.

There's a trap, too. The better a model understands you, the better it predicts what you'd do next. A machine that offers endless plausible variations on what you've already done, every time you get stuck, is both sweet and dangerous. You've effectively raised the world's foremost expert on your own clichés.

So the author's prescription isn't generation. It's to start by organizing the archive, picking out what represents you, starting small, and writing down why you made things the way you did. Choosing the dataset is itself the first artistic act of building a personal AI. The model knows your past, but what it becomes next is still up to the person.

blocks.cap: UMG × Hook

blocks.x: Universal Music Group has entered a licensing partnership with Hook. Hook is an AI-powered remix and mashup app that also includes video-editing tools for social sharing, and fans can now build content using UMG's official recordings.
The announcement came on Wednesday, August 19. It covers licensed user-generated content across social media, with proceeds going back to UMG artists and rights holders.

Hook raised $10 million in February in a Series A led by Khosla Ventures. At the time, the company said it lets people remix songs with AI tools and share them across platforms while protecting artists' ownership and control alongside rights holders.

According to both companies, Hook is different from generative AI platforms. It doesn't generate new songs. It only lets fans create UGC using licensed music. Every creation carries licensing, credit, and tracking, so money flows to UMG artists and rights holders both when fans make something and when that creation spreads.

Artist control sits at the center of the deal. UMG artists and rights holders decide which songs are opened up, which creative features fans can use, and where the results can be posted. Features like remixing, sound effects, and video clipping can also be toggled on or off individually.

"We don't think the biggest consumer use case for music creation is making original songs that compete with the artist. It's expressing yourself through the artists and songs you love, and participating in the community and culture they've built." — Hook founder and CEO Gaurav Sharma

The agreement follows two years of work with UMG labels including Republic Records, Capitol Records, Mavin, and Virgin Music Group. During that time, more than 30 artist campaigns spanning new releases, remixes, and social fan activity were built.

"Streaming changed how fans listen to music. Licensed fan creation is a major pillar of the next chapter. It brings together artist control, responsible technology, and new ways of creating value. This is the kind of innovation we want to lead." — UMG Vice Chairman and Chief Digital Officer Michael Nash

UMG's licensing push has continued apace. In October 2025, it settled a copyright lawsuit with AI music platform Udio and agreed to jointly develop licensed AI music creation services, and in May it renewed a multi-year global licensing agreement with TikTok, expanding AI protections for artists and songwriters.

In December 2025, Hook claimed that a 'Create Hook' feature released by AI music generator Suno too closely resembled its own brand and product. At the time, Hook said the feature "mirrored our identity and functionality closely enough to raise serious concerns about consumer confusion and the protection of Hook's trademarks and brand."

Hook's investors include Khosla Ventures, Point72, Imaginary Ventures, and Waverley Capital, co-founded by former Warner Music Group CEO Edgar Bronfman Jr. In 2024, it also signed a track licensing deal with Downtown Music.

blocks.cap: Tamber 2.0. Image: Tamber

blocks.x: Tamber has released v2.0. The company calls this release a “major expansion” of its music creation platform. It reworked its creative tools, added new features, and now supports Windows natively.

Tamber first launched in May this year, so this update follows fairly quickly. It is a creative suite built on technology the company calls “sonic intelligence,” weighted toward assistance rather than generation. It turns vague thoughts and ideas drifting in your head into sound. It runs natively on both Mac and Windows, sitting alongside the DAW and production tools you already use.

So what has changed? Tamber's five core tools — Gestures, Tamby, Librarian, City Packs, and Sonic Atlas — now each run as a dedicated app within one connected suite. You open the tool you need directly and move between tools under a single account.

Gestures reads your hands through a webcam to control vocal effects and virtual instruments. In v2.0, it works as a standalone instrument and also as a VST3/AU plugin. It gained new synth and vocoder engines inside, and latency has dropped.

Tamby, which calls itself an “in-session co-producer,” is now a non-intrusive overlay you summon when you need it. Chat history is kept, so earlier prompts and work stay preserved. A mini Librarian search bar now floats over the DAW too, along with favorites and crate tools.

City Packs keep growing. These packs are filled with field recordings captured in person, with a new one released every month. Sonic Atlas, the visual exploration app for browsing popular music by country, city, and era, also gained favorites.

Tamber does not generate finished songs, stems, or samples. In a press release sent to MusicTech, the company said it has never trained on third-party audio. Instead, it helps musicians work their own tools. With v2.0, users get greater control over “which parts of Tamber they use, and how those tools fit into their own creative process.”

Founder Zoe Wrenn said: “Almost all of this came from what users told us they needed. Gestures is now a real instrument. With its own synth and vocoder engines, you can play it alone without a DAW, or drop it right into a session as a plugin.”

“Librarian was rebuilt from the ground up, and Tamby picks up right where you left off mid-recording. I've used it in my own sessions for weeks now, and it doesn't feel like an update. It feels like a new product.”

blocks.cap: VAEMI Synterra

blocks.x: VAEMI announced that it will soon release a new standalone “bio-interactive” generative synthesizer. Synterra reads changing data from sources ranging from plants, fungi, and fruit to organic matter, conductive surfaces, light, and human touch, and turns it into music structures that keep growing.

When powered on, a built-in coil reads the surrounding electromagnetic field to set an initial reference point. Because this value shapes the early note distribution and timing behavior, the music keeps changing and never repeats, even when the same source is connected. Resistance changes picked up by probes and light changes received by the onboard LDR turn into events that pass through an internal quantizer and probability engine, generating notes, rhythmic movement, and layered structures within one of eight user-selected scales.

Polyphony can be set anywhere from 1 to 5 voices, and the range spans 5 octaves. Amount and Sensitivity determine how strongly incoming data shakes the system, which decides event density and the overall level of activity in the generative process. There are nine synth patches, covering wavetable and FM synthesis, resonant structures, Karplus–Strong physical modeling, drones, percussive synthesis, and glitch and noise-based sounds.

It works as a standalone instrument, but it isn't tied only to its internal engine. Generated data can be sent to other devices over MIDI, and it has both USB and DIN ports. In MIDI Scale Mode, notes sent from an external keyboard, sequencer, or DAW decide the note material Synterra draws from. The instrument keeps playing on its own but only sounds notes within that incoming set, so it follows the chords and harmonic progression of a song you're already playing or performing live. Switching to Full MIDI Mode skips the generative system entirely, letting you play the internal synth patches directly like any other synthesizer.
Synterra can be pre-ordered now for $99, down from its regular price of $119. The pre-order campaign ends on August 31, 2026, and the first units ship in September 2026.

blocks.cap: Source: Production Expert

blocks.x: Vibe coding, AI-led development, has become standard practice across the software industry. A remark last year from Spotify's co-CEO — “Most senior engineers haven't written a single line of code since December” — shows the approach has moved past its early stage and into top-level development work. So what about the buying side? Can you trust a plugin that AI designed, built, and conceived? Deivids, a developer at Acedia Audio, laid out what vibe coding looks like from both the developer's and the customer's side.

The pitch that you can build an app with a single prompt is still mostly false hope. Building any app through vibe coding requires the developer to deeply understand the project's structure. AI raised development speed, but it also raised the amount of oversight needed by the same measure. That's why AI coding needs to stay focused on narrow areas. Most problems start from getting the scope wrong, and letting AI guess at a plugin's core pillars turns into a large debt right away. The barrier to entry has dropped, but a usable plugin still demands a high level of skill.

There's an upside too. In the past, a single plugin required a large team and a huge budget, so niche ideas always got pushed aside. Now, someone with an idea can build a pitch demo, and sometimes even a finished product. It also becomes possible for sound designers, performers, and Foley artists to build the tools they've long wanted themselves. Using AI to fix up old, unsupported codebases is another great use case. The recent release of the Eleven Rack's silicon driver is one example.

blocks.cap: Source: Production Expert

blocks.x: Companies have adopted this technology at different times and speeds, so even the biggest names in the industry are just starting out in AI development and going through growing pains. The first thing to check is security. A plugin should only need to talk to the outside world for license checks and verification. If it uses a verified third-party provider like PACE, Moonbase, or MuseHub, you can generally feel at ease. If it's a newer company using its own in-house method, it's better to ask the support team directly. How open the support and communication channels are also reveals how long that company plans to stick around.

Performance and stability matter too. Latency or stalls in audio processing turn into accidents right away, and output from a model that doesn't know this narrow domain well leads to crashes or poor optimization. You don't need to run benchmarks. Just grab a trial version and see if it holds up with your workflow and gear. Design is a signal too. Leave the color palette to AI, and it converges on whatever style that model used most often. Claude Opus models had a habit of automatically picking a deep blue-purple palette, and the same color scheme showed up across different people's different projects.

In the end, there are six things to check: whether there's a trial, whether it uses a trustworthy license verification system, whether support channels are open, whether it handles your work without strain, whether the design is distinctive, and whether there's evidence it's been used in real professional settings. You don't need a technical background to judge this. Just ask yourself whether this plugin feels like a person was actually steering it. Vibe coding has raised the ceiling on what a developer can do, and the risk and the promise come from the same shift. In the end, it all depends on how developers use this technology.

blocks.cap: A producer working on a laptop in the studio

blocks.x: MusicTech rounded up this week's new plugins. Several lean on machine learning for stem separation and synthesis, without billing themselves as AI.

WaveMachine Labs' ReStem 2 splits a mixed drum recording into kick, snare, hi-hat, toms, ride, crash, and the rest. Each separated element gets its own level, gating, and dynamics control. It can run in real time or as offline rendering. The kick and snare channels use Drumagog technology for sample replacement. Core costs $99, Pro costs $199.

Minimal Audio's Lucid is a granular synthesizer. It retunes each grain to a scale in real time and stacks grains into chords and arpeggios. It comes with per-grain filtering and imaging, a multi-tap grain delay with scale-locked pitch shifting, animatable-macro modulation, and eight effects. Introductory price is $79, regular price is $129.

blocks.cap: Lucid, Minimal Audio's granular synthesizer

blocks.x: Orph's Monochord is a “dream machine and harmony workstation” that pairs vintage hardware samples with chord programming. It holds 425 sounds drawn from the Fairlight CMI, Memorymoog, Oberheim OB-X, Casio VL-1, Bontempi B3, and Suzuki Omnichord. It adds fifteen effects modeled on gear like the Space Echo and Eventide H3000, more than 600 chord voicings, and an arpeggiator and strum mode. It costs 139 euros.

Gulf Coast Synthesis' Spectral is an additive synthesis instrument for drawing harmonics directly. Dragging audio or an image onto the Spectral Canvas converts it into harmonics, and you can also draw sound by hand with a brush. Pattern and Sacred Geometry generators create spectra, with All, Even, Odd, and Inharmonic modes for selecting overtones. Pitch drift, tape wobble, and dropouts mimic analog texture. Introductory price is $39, regular price is $69.

blocks.cap: OA-Phosphor-1, the free Mac synthesizer from OA-Labs

blocks.x: OA-Labs released OA-Phosphor-1, a free virtual analog synthesizer plugin for Mac.

The developer describes it as a synth for “controllable instability,” and that fits well. Phosphor-1 can produce plain subtractive-synthesis sounds too. But for me, at least, the fun starts when you shake, stretch, wobble, and collapse the sound.
I've said several times that vibe-coded plugins are flooding in these days. Rather than cover everything that lands in the inbox, BPB News tries to focus on the decent free plugins.

Phosphor-1 also got AI help with its coding. That doesn't mean it's a plugin pulled out with a single prompt, though. The developer is a designer and musician, and says refining the interface and dialing in the sound took about two months.
Having used it myself, it's fun to tinker with. If you like sounds that feel like they're coming off a stretched cassette, or the detuned textures in the Boards of Canada vein, it's worth a look.

The core control is Age. It applies across the whole instrument at once. Turning it up makes the pitch, filter, level, and shape all start to wobble together. The motion layered on by the chaos engine never repeats exactly the same way, so you can push it from subtle analog-style flaws all the way to much more unstable states.

That design suits me well. I built BPB Dirty VHS for VHS-style wobble and degradation, and BPB Dirty LA for compression with added grit. Phosphor-1 sits in a similar space, but it's an instrument rather than an effect.

There are two oscillators plus a dedicated sub-oscillator, mixed with cross, ring, and hard sync. A morphing multimode filter moves from low-pass to notch, band-pass, and high-pass, and a waveshaper handles warp, curve, fold, and bias.

A generative arpeggiator also stands out. It goes beyond a simple up-down pattern, adding groove, glitch, and per-step probability. On top of that come dual LFOs, amp/filter/pitch envelopes, poly and mono modes, a legato mode, unison with spread and phase, glide, up to 4x oversampling, a preset browser, and 68 presets.
OA-Labs said it's testing Windows support and taking a waitlist. Reverb and delay, MIDI sync, arp steps that follow a pattern, more presets, and bug fixes could be added down the line.
OA-Phosphor-1 comes as AU and VST3 for Mac. The download is 18MB, and entering an email address gets it for free.

Suno is taking down all the AI models it currently runs. It said it will soon introduce a new generation of models developed together with the music industry, and once that model arrives, every previous model will be retired.

The starting point is a licensing deal with BMG. The agreement, announced on Wednesday, August 12, includes BMG's recordings and publishing repertoire together. It's the first major deal since the Warner settlement in November 2025, though BMG was never a plaintiff in the RIAA lawsuit to begin with. It's framed as settling past use rather than resolving litigation. Suno CEO Mikey Shulman said that building a responsible future means working directly with the people who make music, while BMG's Celine Joshua said choice is the guiding principle.

Starting September 3, downloads become the gateway to commercial release. Free users get seven downloads for life, and even those carry no commercial rights. Pro gets 20 a month, Premier gets 60 a month. Extra downloads can be purchased separately. To put a track on a streaming service, users must first spend one of these downloads. Suno said the move is meant to make it harder for bad-faith users to mass-extract music as the platform grows.

Files carry a watermark that's hard to remove. Audible Magic and Musixmatch have joined as partners, and Suno is the first customer for Sentinel, Musixmatch's new copyright-detection system. The idea is to filter out Suno-made tracks at the point of entry into distribution. Spotify charges 10 euros a month for each track flagged as artificial streaming, and removed more than 75 million spam tracks over the 12 months through September 2025. In mid-September, Suno will also launch an AI Persona badge for AI-made profiles.

Studio 2.0, which opened on August 13, includes MIDI import, recording, editing, stem separation, audio effects and automation, and wavetable synth design. Premier users can export unlimited 32-bit/48kHz multitrack and stems — opening up a pro-tier path outside the download cap. It's built on WavTool, which Suno acquired in September 2025.

On August 6, the Suno Vinyl waitlist opened. It presses up to 46 minutes onto a 12-inch black PETG disc, priced at around $45 before shipping. The company says these aren't novelty-cut discs but properly pressed records — a way to make money that bypasses streaming distribution.

blocks.cap: How to capture AI search results with Preferred Sources — a guide for artists and venues

blocks.x: As Google expands Preferred Sources, artists and venues have gained a new form of leverage. It's a way to claim top placement in AI search, AI Overviews, and AI Mode, and push back against the website traffic that AI has been eroding.

Any site can now embed Google's official Preferred Source button directly. Once a fan clicks that button, Google will prioritize the official domain and prominently attach a 'Preferred' badge whenever that fan later asks an AI search tool about music, show times, or venue rules.

Ticket-information hallucinations drop first. AI answer engines often get show times wrong or send fans toward reseller ticket scams, but once the priority badge is in place, the official domain gets cited as the primary source. Click-through rates change too. Google's own data shows that Preferred Source links in AI search results get clicked roughly twice as often. Generative engine optimization (GEO) usually demands complex technical setup, but this feature converts fan loyalty that's already been built up directly into search authority.

There are three places to use it. Place Google's lightweight JavaScript button on the official site's root domain, near tour or event pages. In presale emails, attach a one-click link asking fans to “save us as a Preferred Source in Google so AI search shows our official ticket links and show times first.” Also put the button at the top of the FAQ page that lists venue rules, entry times, and box-office hours. When a fan asks AI “what's [venue name]'s bag policy,” your site becomes the one that gets cited.

Installation splits two ways. On sites that allow custom HTML/JS, like WordPress or Squarespace, embed Google's interactive button so fans can register in one step without leaving the site. Place a div with the google-add-preferred-source-btn attribute where the button should appear, and add the news.google.com/swg/js/v1/swg-basic.js script tag to the head. Choose data-theme as dark or light to match the site's tone.

If a site builder blocks scripts, or if you'd rather route fans through email, social media, or a link-in-bio, use Google's direct link instead. Just swap in your own root domain at the end of https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=yourdomain.com. When a fan clicks it, they land straight on Google's source settings screen with the domain pre-filled, and one more click finishes it.

The fight for AI visibility no longer comes down to keywords, but to how much of your fan base you've locked in. Adding the button and putting the link in an email takes just a few minutes, but when your most devoted fans ask an AI search tool a question, it's your link that comes back as the answer.

blocks.cap: AI-generated music will be excluded from Australia's ARIA charts. Photo: Johnny Bhalla

blocks.x: Under new rules set by the Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA), songs made entirely or mostly by artificial intelligence will be excluded from Australia's official charts starting this Friday. Recordings that used AI assistance can still chart if they are “substantially human-made,” meaning a person made a substantial part of the song.

ARIA, which runs the charts of Australia's most-listened-to music, revised its chart code of practice to align with principles set by the global recording industry. The new code excludes music made with generative AI in principle, with an exception only for cases that are “substantially human-made” and “raise no stream or chart manipulation concerns.”

ARIA can remove ineligible releases from the charts, change their rankings, and revoke chart awards already given. Artists or their representatives can appeal if they believe a decision is wrong. The rules take effect starting with the chart announced on Friday, August 28.

ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd drew a line between artists already using AI-assisted tools and music generated wholesale by an AI service trained on an artist's recordings, calling the two entirely different issues. Herd said, “this gives everyone releasing music in Australia a clear set of rules to follow.”

Behind the decision is a controversy over a cover of Madonna's 'Like a Prayer' made by Queensland DJ and producer Josh Fawaz. It became the most-played song on Australian radio last month and climbed as high as No. 4 on two ARIA charts, but the industry raised concerns that it used generative AI. Fawaz admitted he used AI “as a tool,” and later updated the track's Spotify credits to say the vocals and drums were AI-generated.

Most of ARIA's changes follow standards the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) released in July. At the time, IFPI said more than 20 official chart programs were adopting rules to distinguish human-made recordings from recordings generated wholesale by AI. An ARIA representative explained that, under IFPI's standards, music with AI-generated lead vocals or core instruments would likely be disqualified. Fawaz's track also looks unlikely to chart going forward.

The move comes amid disputes between creators and AI companies playing out around the world. Several AI companies have used copyrighted material for training without permission, claiming fair use. The Australian government has also said it is developing AI and data center regulations that include “strong copyright protections” for domestic creators.

blocks.cap: An illustration of Cyanite's AI music tagging technology

blocks.x: German startup Cyanite was an early mover in generating music metadata with AI. Music Ally first covered the company in July 2019, when its automated tagging technology spun out of an existing company called Groovecat.
A little more than seven years later, the platform is getting a major overhaul, an upgrade Cyanite calls 'Tagging 2.0.' The core idea, analyzing a music catalog to generate metadata, stays the same.

What's changed is who reads that metadata. It's no longer just humans. The company sees the parties that “explore, organize and actually put catalogs to use” increasingly shifting toward AI systems, a range that spans conversational search and personalized recommendations to catalog automation and intelligent assistants.
Many of the newly reworked features are aimed at this shift. The upgraded system is already in use by clients including BeatStars, The Source, Rambling Records and Human Worldwide.
CEO Markus Schwarzer said, “AI is changing how the music industry works with catalogs. But these new workflows are only as good as the musical understanding underneath them.”

blocks.cap: MiniMax Music 3 — an open-weight model that generates songs up to five minutes long from lyrics and a music description

blocks.x: It's another big day for open source. A top-tier open-weight music generation model has arrived in ComfyUI: MiniMax Music 3, from MiniMax. Give it lyrics and a description of the sound you want, and it returns a complete, structurally coherent song up to five minutes long in 32kHz stereo.

The model is built for generating a whole song, not loops or short clips. Conditioned on lyrics and a music description, it holds onto theme, rhythm, vocal identity, and arrangement progression across the entire track. Output is 32kHz 16-bit stereo audio.

The architecture is a hybrid combining two language models with a continuous synthesis stage. An 8B Global LLM, starting from Qwen3-8B, handles the song's long-range flow and structural progression, while a 0.6B Local LLM restores fine acoustic detail within each frame. Rather than decoding audio from discrete tokens alone, it combines the hidden states of both LLMs and passes them to a 2.4B Flow Matching stage and a 123M Flow-VAE decoder. This continuous representation, which carries acoustic information tokens can't hold, is what makes the difference in vocal pronunciation, instrument texture, and temporal continuity.

Song length up to five minutes is supported by default. It maintains the progression through intro, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, bridge, instrumental, and outro while holding onto melody, rhythm, and vocal identity. In the lyrics input, you set the structure by writing section tags directly, such as [Intro], [Verse], [Pre-Chorus], [Chorus], [Post-Chorus], [Bridge], [Instrumental], [Solo], and [Outro].

Using a Structured Caption instead of a plain description widens the range of control. It splits into Global Metadata, covering genre, BPM, key and scale, emotional progression, and production character; Vocal Details, covering gender, timbre, singing style, harmony, backing vocals, and effects; and Arrangement, covering instrumentation and section-by-section changes in groove, bass, percussion, texture, and spatial feel. Vocals can be tuned down to timbre, harmony, and effects, and thanks to the hidden-state synthesis pathway, pronunciation stays stable even over long stretches. Output is 16-bit stereo WAV, and the Flow-VAE decoder was retrained to match music's dynamic range and spectral characteristics.

MiniMax also released an official skill that converts a short music description and tagged lyrics into a detailed structured caption for Music 3.0. It keeps any stated musical constraints as they are and leaves the lyric text in the lyrics input, while generating a caption that runs through Global Metadata, Vocal Details, and arrangement description section by section. The install command is npx skills add MiniMax-AI/MiniMax-Music3 --skill music-caption-rewriter.

To try it yourself, update ComfyUI to 0.33.0 or use Comfy Cloud instead. Download the workflow or find it in the template library, then follow the workflow's instructions to get the model weights and place them in the designated model folder. Fill in the lyrics and music description and run it, and that's it. The weights are up on Hugging Face at MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3.
Trama, made by Ohlhorst Digital, is a free standalone AI stem separator that runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

StemDeck, which we covered recently, was a free, open-source local separator that split tracks into up to six stems. Trama takes a similar offline approach, but focuses on four stems and packs what's needed into a single desktop app.

Drag in a mixed track and it splits into vocals, drums, bass, and everything else. You can choose and export just the combination you want from the four, and whatever you don't pick gets merged back into a single file. There's no reason to export stems you won't use.

The interface is lean, and installation is simple. There's no account, no cloud upload, and no separate model download. On Windows, you unzip it and run it directly; macOS gets it as a disk image; and on Linux, you just extract the binary and grant it execute permission.

What runs under the hood is htdemucs_ft, a Hybrid Transformer Demucs model fine-tuned by Meta. All four separation models are bundled into the app and loaded into memory at runtime, so the entire process finishes locally with no internet connection needed.

Quality is chosen among Normal, High, and Ultra. Raising the setting runs more separation passes and averages the results, so stems come out cleaner but take longer. Ohlhorst Digital recommends High as a safe default.

For a three-minute song run at High, the developer's figures are 1 to 2 minutes on a compatible NVIDIA GPU and 10 to 15 minutes on CPU. Windows and Linux use CUDA automatically if it's available, but there's no AMD GPU acceleration yet. On Apple silicon, the MPS backend is disabled, so it runs on CPU.

You can also queue up multiple songs to process at once. Progress and estimated completion time are shown per file and for the whole queue. Stem selection, the quality preset, and the output folder are all remembered for next time.

Input accepts WAV, AIFF, MP3, and FLAC. All stems come out as 44.1kHz 32-bit floating-point WAV, and other sample rates get resampled during separation. It also preserves WAV metadata such as BWF data, cue points, labels, playlists, instrument info, ID3 tags, and Reaper markers.

Trama v1.0.7 supports 64-bit Windows 10/11 and x86_64 Linux. On macOS, it requires 12 or later and Apple silicon only, leaving out Intel Macs. Because the models and libraries are bundled in whole, the download sizes are large: about 3.1GB for Windows, 500MB for macOS, and 3.9GB for Linux.

blocks.cap: Chartmetric Flow AI screen

blocks.x: If there's one place in the music industry where AI is being put to real use, it's analytics. Streaming and social data pouring in right up to the minute is great, but reading it is another matter.
So this morning Chartmetric unveiled a new tool, ‘Flow AI.’ The company describes it as “the most powerful vertical AI agent built for music professionals.”
It puts a more approachable prompt interface on top of all that data. CEO Sung Cho says it's “not just another AI chatbot.”

“Ask Flow anything — about your roster, your competitors, or the market. It searches Chartmetric's entire dataset, works through the data, and gives you a clear answer instead of raw numbers.” That's from the Flow website.

Chartmetric isn't the only analytics company digging into what AI can do. We've covered competitor Viberate releasing an MCP server in June, and Soundcharts has one too. Openstage does the same thing on the artist-owned fan data side.
For these companies, AI is both a necessary upgrade and a card that can push revenue higher. A Chartmetric Flow AI subscription starts at $60 a month.

Still, the phrase “instead of raw numbers” leaves one question open, because it's a judgment aimed at how music analytics has worked until now — a setup where raw data flows in, and only becomes action once an expert interprets it and hands it off to colleagues like a marketing team.

Will an AI-powered analytics era grow the work those experts do, reshape their roles into something more interesting, or cut them out of the loop entirely? It's a question a lot of people are facing these days, standing in front of new AI tools that can now do much of what used to be our job.

blocks.cap: Hotone Pulze Jr. — a mini amp with AI inside (Photo courtesy of Hotone)

blocks.x: Hotone's newly released Pulze Jr. is a battery-powered portable mini amp for guitarists. It has an AI feature built in that helps you find the tone you want.

At its core is a CDCM HD & FIRE modeling system squeezed into mini-amp size. It uses 52 amp models, 48 cabinets, and multiple effects. It shares a retro look with the 5-watt Pulze-Mini, and comes in white and black.

blocks.cap: Hotone Pulze Jr., now with AI (Photo courtesy of Hotone)

blocks.x: It also has separate acoustic simulation with matching effects. It stores up to 200 presets. Digital signal processing runs at 24-bit/48kHz, and two 3-inch speakers put out 20 watts in stereo — a solid output given its size.

If you want to widen the sound further, it adds up to 20 user IRs and up to 10 Sound Clone / NAM A1 and A2 files. It suits anyone building a virtual rig with their own cabinet simulations or amp profiles.
There are several extras too: a 240-second looper, a drum machine and metronome combo with 100 rhythms, and a tuner.

This mini amp uses its head, too. A preset-generation feature powered by Hotone AI pulls up the right sound setting at the press of a button. It also includes AI track separation for preparing backing tracks. Management happens through the Hotone Pulze Editor app, and Bluetooth support covers music streaming or wireless app connection as well.
Hotone says the built-in 3000mAh lithium battery lasts about 8 hours playing music continuously at medium volume.
Pricing is £260.00/€299.00. It's an amp that works fine sitting in the living room or carried outside. It'll be available soon at Thomann in black and white.

blocks.cap: Oscar Peterson at a TV performance filmed in London in March 1984 (Photo: David Redfern/Redferns/Getty Images)

blocks.x: If any genre seems hardest for AI to analyze, wouldn't it be jazz, with its improvisation and loose structure? A new paper in Nature Machine Intelligence says otherwise.

The research was led by Huw Cheston at the University of Cambridge. A large language model identified jazz pianists and even revealed the “musical fingerprint” that set each player apart from the others.

Cheston's team fed the machine 1,629 performances by 20 pianists, totaling 84 hours of recordings. The pianists included Bill Evans, Oscar Peterson, Thelonious Monk, Chick Corea, Keith Jarrett, McCoy Tyner, and Ahmad Jamal. The recordings were converted to MIDI and laid out on piano rolls, showing exactly which notes were played, when, and at what pitch.

The results held up well. The best-performing model identified the player with 94.4% accuracy. Testing each element on its own, harmony was the most predictive, followed by rhythm and melody. Dynamics was the least accurate.

So where does this apply in the real world? The researchers see several uses. One is narrowing down candidate authors for unattributed works, or telling genuine recordings from forgeries. It also exposes the web of influence between artists and offers a window into the creative process itself.
The researchers added: “Finally, there's use in education too. It helps train artists to understand the distinctive voices held by major figures in their field.”
To dig deeper into the research, head to the Nature Machine Intelligence site. There's also a web app that lets you browse each pianist's playing style directly.

blocks.cap: Luminate, an entertainment data company (Photo courtesy of Luminate)

blocks.x: On Tuesday, August 25, entertainment data company Luminate rolled out a new framework for handling AI music. Starting in the second half of this year, it will begin labeling AI-generated content on its own platform, and that label will be shown directly to client and partner companies as well.

This comes just weeks after Apple Music and Spotify each said they'd apply their own AI music labeling by the end of 2026. Luminate combines its own identification technology with collaboration from major streaming services and AI music companies to decide which songs get labeled. Songs or artist profiles the system flags carry an “AI Generated” mark, and if that's a false positive, artists and labels can go through a dedicated review process to have the label reconsidered.
In the framework, Luminate CEO Rob Jonas wrote, “This is a starting point. No single organization can handle this issue alone,” and broke the labeling approach into three parts.

The proprietary identification system constantly scans streaming data and metadata, adding audio identification tools to track AI-generated music within CONNECT. On the streaming-data side, it absorbs that data through existing partnerships as DSPs roll out their own AI music identification features. Source attribution targets the stage before a song or artist ever reaches a DSP, working directly with AI music companies to obtain attribution data from the moment content is created.

The labeling debate goes back to early 2025. Last January, Deezer tagged tracks made 100% with AI, and several others followed this year. Spotify marks “AI Personas” instead of tracks, and Apple Music will apply AI labels later this year based on self-disclosure. The record industry that supplies songs to streaming services also said in July that it supports AI labeling measures.
Some have taken a different path. Even as labeling AI music has become the dominant approach to the flood of AI content, Bandcamp and iHeartRadio have banned music that's mostly AI-made outright.

Jonas said this about the new framework: “The industry's ability to identify and measure AI-generated music hasn't kept pace with how fast it's multiplying. Visibility needs to improve so we can read the bigger trends, gauge fraud risk, and make sound judgment calls. Luminate has always been the standard of truth for the entertainment industry. Tracking AI-generated music by the same yardstick we apply to every other category is at the core of our mission.”

blocks.cap: Steinberg SpectraLayers Pro 13 — a boost in modules for dialogue correction and audio restoration

blocks.x: With new and reworked modules arriving together, SpectraLayers Pro 13 stands out especially for people doing post-production work like dialogue correction, audio restoration, or sound design. Steinberg's spectral editor has opened up an even wider set of processing options.

Spectral editing has come a long way over the past five years. Both the features themselves, like stem separation and unmixing, and the way users handle demanding audio-processing tools, have improved a great deal. Underneath it all is the rapid progress of machine learning and AI.

That's also why Steinberg updates SpectraLayers Pro every year. SpectraLayers Pro 13 arrived right on the heels of v12, which SOS covered in its October 2025 issue. There are several new processing modules, but there's also no shortage of polish to the workflow and UI.

If v12 put its weight on music-side unmixing, v13 shifts the focus to post-production work like voice and dialogue processing and audio restoration. The newly added Reconstruct module resynthesizes the spectral data within a file. Its predecessor, Heal, only brought back background noise, but Reconstruct looks at the material surrounding the area to be restored and rebuilds transients and tonal content as well. For small sections, like spots where noise has been removed, its skill at filling in both signal and noise together is quite impressive.

The new Ambience Heal module is no less capable. It proves especially useful after running an unmixing pass that pulls dialogue away from the background, which leaves a hole in the background layer. Ambience Heal reads information from the foreground layer holding the extracted voice to point out exactly where the background layer needs fixing.
