After cleaning up or replacing vocals and laying them back over an evenly filled background, the result comes out noticeably smoother.
From the following Speak To… section onward, access is limited to Sound On Sound subscribers.
ElevenLabs has released Composer, a section-based song editor built into ElevenMusic, the generative AI music platform it launched earlier this year.
The starting point is open: bring your own lyrics or track, start from a single-line prompt, or begin with a blank screen. From there, you refine the piece section by section.
“Now artists and creators can rewrite a verse, change the chorus, slow down the bridge, and try different versions, without touching the parts that already work,” said an ElevenLabs spokesperson.
“Put simply, this tool lets you edit a song the way you edit a document.”
In the company's own words: “Music is rarely finished in one pass. You might like the verse but want a different chorus, or the melody is right but the lyrics need to change.”

“Composer lets you handle those decisions separately. You can edit and regenerate any section of a track without changing the rest, adjusting the style, tempo, energy, instrumentation, key, and length of the section you're working on while leaving everything else in place.”
The overall structure is also within reach. You can swap in a new bridge, double the chorus, add an outro, and rearrange the order section by section.

The news comes as ElevenLabs passed $500 million in annual revenue earlier this year. Its Series D round brought in actors Jamie Foxx and Eva Longoria, Hwang Dong-hyuk, the director of “Squid Game,” and BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, as new investors.
This puts ElevenLabs a step closer to its biggest rivals, Suno and Udio. The funding round was first reported in February at an $11 billion valuation.

Symphonic virtual instruments are heard in dramas and, occasionally, in blockbuster soundtracks. Their use isn't limited to that. They also bring in strings and horns for hip-hop, rock, and pop arrangements without a big budget.

Until now, these tools came with a cost. They are complex to learn and heavy to run. It was common to load terabytes of samples while using only a handful of articulations and mic positions. Hard drives, CPUs, and credit card limits all melted together.

Dreamtonics has wrapped up its virtual instrument trilogy with Instrument X. It calls itself a professional neural acoustic modeling platform. It builds sound inside the DAW using neural synthesis and ethically licensed performer performances. It doesn't use a single sample.

blocks.cap: Dreamtonics Instrument X, which makes sound without samples.

blocks.x: The requirement is 8GB of RAM. Instrument expansion packs number up to 15, and none exceeds 150MB. It comes as a standalone and a plugin, supporting both standard formats and ARA. Dreamtonics recommends an ARA bridge mode that attaches an ARA instance to an audio track carrying dummy audio.

Articulations have no keyswitches. They shift automatically based on pitch and length, and stack expression lets you layer special techniques. AI retakes let you regenerate an entire sequence or tweak only values like timbre drift, pitch curve, and dynamic intensity.

The spatial mixer runs 8 to 11 channel mic configurations through neural acoustics. You can weigh positions from close mics to a Decca tree to ambient room pairs. The spatial character here isn't algorithmic reverb; it's a real acoustic profile Dreamtonics captured at a “high-end tracking studio” in Tokyo.

It takes in MusicXML and carries tempo, time signature, articulation, and dynamics straight into performance data. It also connects with Synthesizer V Studio 2 Pro and Vocoflex. That said, this article is partner content from Production Expert. It's better to judge by listening for yourself.

blocks.cap: sonible smart:chain (photo courtesy of sonible)

blocks.x: In sonible smart:chain, the processing chain pulls information from multiple instances across the DAW, giving a level of control that hasn't existed before.

The Austrian developer sonible is known for AI-assisted processing plugins for mixing and mastering. Under Audiotonix, it sits alongside SSL and Harrison Audio, and has recently collaborated on projects like SSL's autoSeries.

This time, sonible has expanded its flagship smart Series line of content-aware processing plugins by adding smart:chain. It's an intelligent mixing processor that works as multiple nodes across the whole DAW. It gathers compression, EQ, gating, saturation, gain riding, de-hissing, and auto leveling cleanly into one screen, letting you bring forward the elements that matter in the mix.

Channel strip plugins are nothing new, but smart:chain takes a different approach. Instead of each processing chain running on its own, the plugin instances interlock to set an appropriate starting point for each module. It also comes with intelligent depth layering, pushing elements to the front, middle, or back of the mix to create balance, separation, and depth.

Auto Leveling, which runs across the whole session, is also useful. It reads the relationships between elements in the mix and sets a rough mix suited to the musical style. For channel-by-channel tweaks, there's a dedicated trim control. Inside smart:chain, you move between individual channels, manage channel groups, and adjust plugin instances one by one from a central session control screen.

blocks.cap: sonible smart:chain (photo courtesy of sonible)

blocks.x: Competition in this space has gotten interesting too. FabFilter's Instance List gives quick access to every plugin instance in the DAW, but sonible has gone a step further: instead of individual plugins each processing on their own, it acts on the mix as a whole.

The sonible smart:chain plugin is on sale at an introductory price of 99 euros (regular price 179 euros) until September 28, 2026. A crossgrade is also available for those who already own smart Series plugins.

blocks.cap: Gina Jones (photo courtesy of SoundOn)

blocks.x: “TikTok is signing AI music creators now? Saw that coming.” That's the kind of reaction you might hear from some corners of the music industry at today's news that SoundOn, TikTok's distribution arm, has signed a new deal.

But the story of Gina Jones, who lives in Tennessee, and her “Gina's Pet Bangers” series is more complicated than that. It's also a snapshot of just how tricky it has become to draw the line between what is and isn't “AI music” in 2026.
Start with Gina herself. Her bio says she has “worked as a Nashville songwriter for over 30 years, signed three record deals, and been mentored by legends like country songwriter Harland Howard.”

Recently, she has taken a sharp turn. Written with her daughter and granddaughter, these are “songs where country meets hip-hop, inspired by ugly-but-cute dogs.” Tracks like “Chippy Dippy Doppie Duck” and “Leeda Beeda Boda Butt” fall into this category.
Anyone who has followed the AI music trend over the past two years might hear it for the first time and think, “That's definitely made with Suno.”
Jones herself describes her method as “an AI hybrid production approach that combines my original songwriting and melodies with modern production and voice-cloning technology.”

After her songs gained traction on TikTok, she posted a video laying out her process in more detail. “I bring in family members and we write the lyrics together. I come up with the melody myself. I sing and play it, then put it into an AI program.”

What comes next is the key part. “I clone my voice into that program, type in the melody, and specify everything a producer would do — the sound I want, the BPM — line by line.” She made clear she has never hidden the fact that she uses AI.

There's one more layer that feels distinctly 2026: Genni, an influencer marketing firm for music and entertainment. Known as Songfluencer until a year ago, it has handled campaigns for Sabrina Carpenter, Tate McRae, and Doja Cat, and this time it pushed the virality of the “Pet Bangers” series.

Jones' monthly Spotify listeners have just topped 42,000, and her most-streamed track on the platform, “Emerald Jade Green Ball,” has racked up 723,000 plays. Her TikTok account, Gina's Pet Bangers, has 12,500 followers.

That leaves a question. Under the “AI-generated” and “AI-assisted” labeling scheme recently proposed by industry groups, where would these songs fall? By Jones' own account, it would be the latter, but the groups' definition — “lead vocal performance AI-generated, core instrumental performance AI-generated” — points to the former. There's also the chart rules' requirement that a track be “meaningfully human-created” and that “any generative AI service used must be properly authorized and lawful.”

What today's news shows is that this issue can't be reduced to a simple yes-or-no on “AI music.” As Suno and its rivals keep changing at the pace of AI, uncertainty is only growing at the very moment the industry is trying to pin down the rules.

blocks.cap: Neural DSP Quad Cortex (photo: Neural DSP)

blocks.x: Neural DSP has released its biggest-ever CorOS update, adding sounds and features to the Quad Cortex amp modeler and multi-effects platform, and expanding guitar plugin compatibility.
CorOS 4.1.0 is free for both Quad Cortex and Quad Cortex Mini users. There's a lot to dig into, but the headline is eight new virtual devices.

They include the Multivoicer harmonizer, the Glitch granular delay, Ring Modulator, Arpeggio Delay, Crystal Delay, Vintage Digital Reverb, and the Douglas Shining compressor and Plugin Parametric-4 EQ, both based on Dark Glass Electronics' Hyper Luminal.

The number of X plugins that can run natively on the device has also grown. Signature Archetype bundles from Tim Henson, John Mayer, John Petrucci, Rabea Massaad and Misha Mansoor have been added to the compatibility list.

Dual Footswitch Assignments is also new, making Quad Cortex's Stomp Mode more usable onstage. Cortex Control 4.1.0 is no small update either: it can control multiple devices from one computer at once, with each unit named so you can switch between them without touching a cable.

blocks.cap: Neural DSP Quad Cortex Mini

blocks.x: Device Presets might be the most interesting part. You can save the settings of any virtual device in your rig and pull them into a different preset.

If you have a US-style boutique clean tube amp dialed in on one preset, you can pull it out and load it directly into another preset. The same goes for virtual speaker cabinets, drives, effects and utilities. Finding a new electric guitar tone has gotten a bit easier. CorOS 4.1.0 ships with 2,000 factory Device Presets.

Francisco Cresp, Neural DSP's CPO and co-founder, called it a “major milestone” for the Quad Cortex ecosystem, giving “musicians more freedom to create, experiment and move between software and hardware without compromise.”
Cortex Control 4.1.0 also got a workflow refresh. Along with Device Presets, it supports I/O Settings Presets and Global EQ Presets.

CEO and co-founder Douglas Castro said: “Every CorOS release makes Quad Cortex a more powerful creative platform. This update is the biggest one we've shipped — not just because of the number of new features, but because it fundamentally changes how fast musicians can create sounds, move between devices, and bring our entire plugin ecosystem into a hardware workflow.”
The update is free.

blocks.cap: Universal Music's AI patent licensing (photo: Brecht Corbeel)

blocks.x: Thirteen months after announcing it would “significantly expand” a patent portfolio through a joint venture formed with Liquidax Capital, Universal Music Group has formally licensed those AI patents to Udio and GRAI.

The UMG-Liquidax joint venture is called Music IP Holdings. The company disclosed the two deals in an official statement sent to DMN. According to the statement and its website, it already holds more than 24 patents, with over 50 more pending.

“This portfolio spans the entire lifecycle of creating, licensing and commercializing AI-generated content — from the moment a prompt is entered through moderation, watermarking, identifier tagging, approval, license distribution, and settlement across open and closed ecosystems,” Music IP Holdings said.
The intent to monetize is clear. The same site hosts a detailed application form for “qualified organizations” seeking to license the patents.

It's no surprise that Udio came in early. The generative AI platform, which once faced off against UMG in court, is now building licensed products with the major label, along with Warner Music and Merlin. Sony Music is not involved.

GRAI is relatively less known. It's an AI-powered remix and social listening app based in Warsaw, and it closed a $9 million seed round led by Khosla Ventures last April. Khosla also holds stakes in Hook and Splash; Hook recently signed a “milestone” deal with UMG.

What happens to companies that don't want to pay? Infringement lawsuits also appear to be on the table — an interesting twist for an industry that has long stood on the other side of patent litigation.

The site states plainly that using the patented technology without a license is infringement, even if a company wrote its own code. In Music IP Holdings' view, technology that “generates music,” “transforms audio into new structures,” “uses new audio workflows,” or “analyzes or decomposes music” requires a license.

So would companies like Klay Vision or Spotify also need to sign patent deals? Time will tell. Based on the website and a Music Row office that quietly opened last November, the joint venture appears to be seeking more deals here.

Bill Campbell's Barefoot Media is helping bring the portfolio to market and develop licensing opportunities across the tech and creative industries. Campbell said, “At every major inflection point in digital music, the most successful models have been the ones that brought technology companies and rights holders together under a clear, practical licensing framework.”

Daniel Drolet, CEO of Music IP Holdings and Liquidax, framed artist protection and innovation together. “This portfolio is designed to do both — opening new opportunities for responsible innovation while giving artists, songwriters and rights holders stronger protection and the right to share in the value their work creates.”

blocks.cap: Dawesome Abyss II (image courtesy of Dawesome)

blocks.x: Developer Dawesome has released Abyss II, a visual synthesizer for macOS and Windows. The introductory price is €89, with a regular price of €149.

Dawesome describes Abyss II as a synth made for musicians rather than engineers. Instead of digging through pages dense with technical parameters to build up a sound, you place visible Tone Colors on a Gradient and move between them to morph the timbre.

The concept itself carries over from the first-generation Abyss, but this version adds one major new way to create sound material. Drop an audio file directly onto the Gradient, and Abyss II turns it into a row of spectral Tone Colors.
The interesting part is that this isn't ordinary sample playback. It analyzes the original and reinterprets it as playable, pitch-accurate synth material.

You can drop a single file or an entire folder onto the Palette view. Abyss II uses machine learning to extract Tone Colors and groups similar results together, building a personal palette out of your own recordings or sample library.
It catches wavetables automatically, and sorts other sources anywhere along the range between organic material and static, wavetable-like material.

Once colors land on the Gradient, the Position control sweeps through those timbres, and the synth's modulation system adds movement. For further sound shaping, there's FM and a virtual analog filter, plus new additions Syntify, Brute, and Velvet, which sharpen, distort, or smooth out a sound.

A new modular effects engine has also been added, with 20 module types across four reorderable slots. A new polyrhythmic sequencer sets step lengths independently, and the package adds full MPE support, three LFOs, two ADSR envelopes, a mono mode, undo and redo, and more than 400 presets.
The presets include around 200 newly made ones alongside around 200 reworked from the first-generation Abyss.

The trial has a low barrier to entry. You can get it without entering an email or creating an account, and the same installer runs in demo mode. The only limitation is that after two or three days, occasional LP-style crackle noise starts creeping in.
If you own Abyss 1, you can upgrade for €45 instead of the regular €75 during the introductory promotion. Anyone who bought Abyss 1 in 2026 gets the upgrade for free.
Abyss II runs on 64-bit Windows 10 and 11 in VST3 and AAX formats. On Intel and Apple silicon Macs running macOS 13 or later, it supports AU, VST3, and AAX.

blocks.cap: Photo: Jason Rosewell

blocks.x: Actors and musicians sent a letter to the UK government. They are asking for better protection against AI cloning and using their voices.

More than 80 performers signed on, including actor Hugh Bonneville and singer Sandi Thom. They asked Prime Minister Andy Burnham to pass a law that would better protect everyone in the UK from voice cloning and the unconsented training of recordings.
Audiobook narrator Alice Sockett, who co-founded the campaign, called voice cloning “an existential threat to our entire industry.”
“My voice is out there, but it has no protection,” she said. “I see voice theft increasing every week.”
Among the signatories is Siobhan McSweeney, an actor from <Derry Girls>. She worried that the government cannot keep pace with how fast AI technology is advancing.
“There is a way to work alongside AI, using it as a tool that benefits us instead of making us obsolete,” she said. “What audiences want is human connection, not AI.”

Scottish singer Sandi Thom, known for her 2006 hit “I Wish I Was a Punk Rocker (With Flowers in My Hair),” explained why she signed the letter, saying her voice is “something that belongs only to me and that I was given at birth.”
“Behind that voice are the emotions, the life, the pain, the tears and the joy I felt getting here,” she added. “Without creativity, we are nothing.”

A government spokesperson told the BBC that “digital replicas can be a powerful tool, including for the creative industries,” but added that there remains room for harm. “We respect and protect human creators. That is why we have announced a public consultation on how to address these harms while protecting legitimate innovation.”

Months earlier, lawyers had warned that AI technology was advancing so fast that UK law had become “not fit for purpose.” AI legal consultant Dr. Mathilde Pavis said, “The law gets close, but it does not fully protect your voice, your face or your identity.”

Voice cloning technology itself has clear uses, such as for people who have lost their voice to illness. The point of this effort is to put legal safeguards in place so that people's voices are not misused as the technology advances.

Cynthia Ju made an important point in an earlier Hypebot piece, “'Human First' Is a Promise Nobody Can Verify Yet.” Her point: claiming a recording is “human first” without any way to back it up is just a line anyone can say. As she puts it, “A claim is visible. What makes it credible is enforcement.”

blocks.cap: Hypebot

blocks.x: Ju traces the history of open-source software, explaining that it mattered because its definition was managed outside the companies that profited from it. But her proposed fix is simply adding a checkbox to the upload forms of distributors like DistroKid, CD Baby, and TuneCore. The logic: self-declaration becomes part of the contract between artist and distributor, giving it legal weight, while enforcement runs at “near-zero marginal cost.”

That is where it runs into reality. What happens when a distributor tells a customer their human-made claim is false, pulls the music from streaming platforms, and cuts off their service? Right there, zero marginal cost turns into investigations, demands for evidence, published standards, appeals processes, and expensive litigation. With no industry consensus and no federal regulation, a rejected artist can simply move to another distributor.

What exactly gets verified before enforcement is also unclear. Is it entirely human-made, partly, or a mix of human and machine? Does a mastering plugin that has sold for over a decade suddenly make a recording AI-made just because it is now marketed as AI? And where do tools that swap a performer's timing and pitch for machine-decided “perfect” values fit in?

The author, Jeffrey Anthony, founded the Musical Form Institute and has worked on this issue. His Certificate of Embodied Production (CEP) is neither a voluntary label nor a checkbox. It is a certification mark filed for registration with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office under serial number 99559776, certifying that a recording was made without grid correction, pitch correction, or generative AI. That does not mean the USPTO certifies individual recordings or approves the CEP standard.

blocks.cap: Certificate of Embodied Production

blocks.x: It belongs in the same category as Certified Organic, Fair Trade, and LEED. A certifying body publishes its standards, evaluates applicants against them, manages who is eligible to use the mark, and maintains enforcement, suspension, and revocation procedures. CEP has the same: published standards, an evidence-review process, conflict-of-interest controls, a public registry, a permanent audit trail, and appeals, suspension, and revocation procedures. A trained human analyst reviews every recording directly.

CEP is not a strict “no AI” label, nor does it push analog purism. It allows assistive processing such as mastering or EQ-helper plugins, because technology alone does not tell you where authority over musical form lies. The three processes are grouped together for one reason: all three take authority over the final form away from the person who performed it.

Distributors can carry certification status in metadata and act when the mark is misused. But the definition, review, and judgment of that claim must stay outside any company that profits from every upload. A checkbox only means something when it points to a real certification process beyond itself.

With AI-made music flooding in, how streaming services should handle these tracks has become the music industry's most urgent question. Opinions diverge on whether to exclude them from royalty payouts, take them down entirely, or simply label them. Billboard has compiled a continuously updated list of each platform's self-disclosed policies.

blocks.cap: Photo: Getty Images

blocks.x: The scale alone is striking. Deezer said in June 2026 that AI tracks made up more than 50% of daily uploads “at peak.” Apple Music told Billboard in April that “more than a third” of its monthly uploads were 100% AI-generated. Qobuz said in January that 34% of new uploads were AI. Tracks that use AI only partially are far harder to catch, so these figures may understate the real scale.

In April 2026, Spotify opened a way for creators to disclose in the credits exactly where AI was used, whether it's a single guitar riff or an entire production. It also rolled out a verification badge for human creators and an artist-profile protection feature that locks artist pages against stray uploads. In August, it announced an “AI persona” label for AI-generated artists, taking effect from mid-September; music carrying that label is excluded from personalized recommendations.

Apple Music will apply its “Made With AI” label, announced in August, by the end of 2026. Labels and distributors tag tracks as “substantially AI-generated,” so the label relies on disclosure rather than automatic detection. YouTube also requires disclosure and applies a label when generative AI content is uploaded, but otherwise has no policy aimed specifically at music.

Tidal has taken the toughest stance. Since June, it has excluded AI-generated content from royalties and placed the responsibility for identifying it on distributors before upload; it began adding labels in mid-July as well. Deezer uses an AI detector to label tracks and exclude them from recommendations, and since July it removes AI tracks suspected of being used for streaming fraud or that haven't been played in over six months. In January, Bandcamp banned outright any track whose creation process used AI entirely or “substantially.”

SoundCloud blocks AI content that impersonates human artists or clones their voices. Amazon Music has only tools for impersonation and spam, with no AI-specific policy yet. Qobuz issued a “human first” stance in January, stating that its playlists, articles, and reviews are 100% human-made.

Round Hill Music has filed copyright infringement lawsuits against Suno and Anthropic in the United States, the latest music rights holder to join the ranks targeting AI companies. The Suno suit also names the Israeli company Bright Data as a defendant, alleging that Suno used Bright Data's tools to illegally scrape millions of songs from digital platforms like YouTube to build its training data.

blocks.cap: Complete Music Update

blocks.x: Round Hill CEO Josh Gruss said, “We are not against artificial intelligence,” but added, “We are against the idea of building multibillion-dollar businesses on other people's creative work and paying creators nothing.” On the obligation to secure licenses, he said it is “not a barrier to innovation” but exists only “to protect the legal owners of the raw material.” He added that, as an independent music company, Round Hill has both the freedom and the duty to say so clearly and act on it.

Round Hill describes itself as “a pioneering private equity platform managing a $1.1 billion music rights portfolio.” It runs investment funds that hold those rights, while also managing the music and turning it into revenue as both a label and a publisher.

Both companies are already facing other lawsuits, so the legal arguments are familiar. Suno has signed licensing deals with Warner Music and BMG, but is still fighting lawsuits from Universal Music, Sony Music, and independent musicians. Anthropic settled a lawsuit from book authors for $1.5 billion, and music publishers have also sued it, alleging it copied lyrics en masse while building training data for Claude.

The core claim in both cases is the same: that the two companies copied recordings and songs Round Hill owns and manages, without a license, to train their respective models. Like other AI companies, Suno and Anthropic hold that AI training is fair use under U.S. copyright law, requiring no permission or license from creators and rights holders.

Some early rulings, including in the authors' case against Anthropic, found that AI training could be fair use. Round Hill argues that defense does not hold up in this case. One reason is the companies' “indefinite retention of unauthorized copies.” It argues that “permanently stockpiling and maintaining a mass of copyrighted works without deciding how they will be used in the future fails every factor of the fair-use analysis,” because “the purpose is acquisition, not transformation.”

The lawsuits are being handled by music industry attorney Richard Busch. He said, “The question in these cases is not complicated,” noting that “copyrighted works were used to build multibillion-dollar businesses — in Anthropic's case, a company valued at more than a trillion dollars — while the songwriters and publishers who created the foundation of that value received nothing.” He added that “there is nothing fair about that use,” and that he intends to make that argument before the court and jury.

Stem separation has moved, in just a few years, from a technology held by a handful of companies to a feature anyone can use. StemDeck shows that shift directly: it's a free, open-source stem-separation app that runs on Linux, Mac, and Windows.

blocks.cap: StemDeck

blocks.x: It's a stem-extraction platform built to separate vocals, drums, bass, piano, and guitar. It's meant for practice, transcription, remixing, and other audio work.
Drag in an MP3, WAV, FLAC, OGG/Opus, MP4, or M4A file, or paste a YouTube link, and it splits the audio into up to six parts: vocals, drums, bass, guitar, piano, and everything else.

After the split, you can listen right away in a multitrack mixer that resembles a DAW. You can mute and solo tracks, adjust levels, zoom in on waveforms, loop sections, and export stems individually or as whatever mix you want. All processing happens entirely on your own computer.

It bills itself as a free alternative to cloud stem-separation services like Moises or LALAL.AI. There's no account, no quota, no upload, and no subscription. It doesn't store, cache, or redistribute downloaded content, and no file ever leaves your device.

The developer drew a clear line: “If you need stems for personal study and want something free and local, StemDeck is enough. If you need a polished finish, a mobile app, or deeper tools for performers, a commercial product is the better choice.”
It's available for download on GitHub, with no price attached.
Suno is deliberately adding friction to the AI overproduction it created. According to Variety, it has imposed a download cap, fencing in how much music users can pull out.

blocks.cap: Image: made with Canva Pro

blocks.x: Streaming services have pulled down millions of tracks suspected of being spam. TechRepublic reports that Spotify is introducing an AI persona label. According to Music Business Worldwide, Suno has also signed a licensing deal with BMG. The view of AI as a bull in a china shop is shifting toward something the music industry embraces, manages, and turns into revenue.

What's left as the real homework is culture. The answer doesn't lie in using AI to mass-produce more creators. MIDiA argues the music industry needs to redefine itself, not as a music business, but as a culture-based one. Rather than producing music and rights, the structure that generates culture through artists is itself the asset that endures in the AI era.

AI's functional capability isn't up for debate. Making a recording has dropped from a task requiring expert skill to a single prompt. In most industries, function is king, and value is priced on end-to-end efficiency and capability. Music is different. It's not a functional industry that extracts raw material, but a cultural industry that carries meaning and identity. The better AI fills music's functional demands, the less that function can set music apart as a cultural asset.

Recordings were, for a long time, a scarce cultural object. Warner Music CEO Robert Kyncl called music “the most abundant thing in the universe besides oxygen” (Semafor). But as recordings flooded in, music lost the cultural asset it alone used to hold. In solving the functional problem of production, a cultural problem was created. The cultural value hasn't disappeared, it has just moved. Power now shifts to where trust already exists: to artists who push forward through performance, history, and personality.

Music now runs on the same track as entertainment as a whole. Athletes, podcasters, influencers, and celebrities occupy the same attention economy as artists. Simply producing and releasing a recording no longer generates achievement, an established audience, or cultural authority.

The power to grow culture comes not from technology but from social infrastructure. MIDiA points to Stockholm as a model. Decades of investment in music education, support studios, venues, and public institutions let the scene grow and let its talent punch above its weight on the global stage. Stockholm is now applying this model to its Meatpacking District, using music as “an engine of urban renewal” (Fast Company).
AI has made music production commonplace. In its place, building culture may become the most valuable skill in the music industry.

You write, record, fix it, mix it, doubt it again, and finally finish mastering — and one day, someone finally says it: this is the master, it's done, nobody touch it. For most of recording history, that moment was sacred. The master was the final authority, the definitive version, the very thing that carried over to records, tapes, CDs, and streaming.

The writer argues that premise is becoming optional, because technology that lets a recording keep changing after release is taking hold. Arrangement, length, mix, and instrumentation can all shift. Someday a recording will respond to who's listening, where, when, and what they're doing.

It's worth remembering that music was originally like this. A performance happened, vanished, and happened again. The same piece differed from last night to tonight. Recording technology captured that event and made it repeatable exactly, and at some point we mistook that capability for a definition. Brian Eno saw the limit a long time ago — the idea that instead of composing every event, you could compose a system that generates events, which led to Generative Music 1 and Reflection.

Bronze treated a song not as a single line running from start to finish, but as a bundle of elements that move during playback. Gwilym Gold's Tender Metal and Jai Paul's “Jasmine” existed that way. Massive Attack's Fantom app responded to information like movement, location, time, and heart rate. Björk's Kórsafn installation took outside weather as an input. Endel goes further, making music that flows according to your condition.

That doesn't turn the listener into a composer. The artist still sets the language of the music, and the listener only enters as one variable inside the system. The industry is what runs into trouble. The record business was built on nouns that count still objects — song, recording, album, master — while the technology is starting to produce things that behave like verbs. You can't attach an identifier to a million variations one by one.

The concern is real too. The way we relate to a recording leans on repetition. You hear a record at nineteen, and hear it again at thirty-five, and at sixty. The record stays the same; what changes is you. That fixedness is what makes it possible to say “that was our song.” Music endlessly reshaped to taste could tilt toward a cultural isolation where no one hears the same thing.

The edges are already coming loose. Apple Music Sing lets you adjust the vocal level on millions of songs, and tools like AutoMix no longer treat a song's beginning and end as untouchable. Spotify is moving toward licensed generative remix and cover tools aimed at commercial recordings. Distributors are shifting from delivering a record to delivering the ability to change one.

So the master of the future may not be a single WAV file, but a system that knows what a song can become: the bass can be swapped but not the lead vocal, the tempo can move within 5 percent, the harmony stays fixed. Writing those rules becomes as important as writing the notes. That doesn't mean the definitive version disappears. Some works get carved in stone, and some move like weather. Deciding which one your work is becomes the artist's call.

blocks.cap: Jimmy Iovine and Dr Dre

blocks.x: The two most influential people in modern music have come out in favor of AI in music.

That's Jimmy Iovine and Dr Dre. The two dug fairly deep into the technology in an interview with The New York Times. Iovine didn't hold back. “I'm very pro-AI in music creation. I don't see a downside. Bad music will come out of it — there's bad music now too. Talented people with AI in the studio in their hands are going to make better records.”

“AI companies are running the worst PR campaign in world history,” he noted. “I don't know all of world history, but I'll say this: the communication has been terrible. That's why everyone's up in arms.”
Dre took it in stride. “I don't see it as a threat. I think the only people who see it as a threat are people who have trouble creating.”

To this producer, AI just seems like new gear. “I was talking to a few people the other day. They were against AI. So I told them, ‘You know, you sound like someone who would've been against the drum machine when it first came out.’ Or the synthesizer. It's a new tool for creating. Some people are scared to learn something new. I'm on the side of embracing it. I'm genuinely curious what's going to happen next.”

The two have worked together since the early 1990s. Iovine's Interscope label backed Dre's solo albums, and those albums rewrote the grammar of hip-hop. In the 2000s, they built the Beats By Dre headphone brand, which Apple acquired in 2014.
Both said they use AI. Iovine thinks there are plenty of producers who are “closeted” users. “They're using it, they just don't want to admit it,” Dre added.

Iovine admitted he uses it all day. Asked what he last asked it, he rattled off a list. “The last thing I asked was how democratic socialism is working out. I also asked about David Byrne's setlist. And about iron absorption in the body, and its timing. Speaking of iron, shrimp or tuna?”
What Dre asked about was how to build muscle and lose fat. But he said the chatbot told him “nothing I didn't already know.”

blocks.cap: CEDAR Audio Voxis

blocks.x: The Icons line CEDAR Audio launched in 2025 started with the idea of opening up the company's restoration tools to a wider base of users. It bundles plugins for live sound and broadcast alongside ones for music production, and this new release belongs to the former group.

Voxis is a voice isolator with under 10ms of latency. It's tuned for situations like conferences, concerts, and sports broadcasts, where engineers have to wrestle with troublesome background noise. It's built on a deep neural network CEDAR has been developing until recently, which the company says separates human speech and vocals from noise at a level that would have been out of reach just a few years ago. The interface is simple: noise reduction is split across low, mid, and high bands, and a Voice control pushes the isolated voice to sound even clearer.

The features the maker highlights are noise removal through neural processing, removal of unwanted reverb, under-10ms latency, processing efficiency that holds up even with multiple instances running, and simple operation. It's aimed at live sound, broadcast, podcasts, worship, house mixing, and post production.

CEDAR Audio CEO Andy Trott said: “Voxis is the third new plugin we've launched this year, as we continue to deliver on our 2026 product roadmap, which includes both new hardware and creative software. As the company that invented digital dialogue noise suppression, CEDAR has built unmatched expertise. We keep turning that deep knowledge and understanding into professional solutions that deliver outstanding results and are a pleasure to use.”
It supports PCs running Windows 10 or later and Macs running macOS 10.13 or later. VST23, AU, and AAX versions are available. It costs £238.80 including VAT and is available now.

blocks.cap: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Max Harris, Getty Images

blocks.x: As generative audio tools grow more sophisticated, the internet is filling up with music that algorithmically pulls melodies and vocals from human artists' work. Some creators admit to using AI right away; others only come clean once the questioning gets intense.

In a scene as closely tied to technology as electronic dance music, what counts as “real” is an urgent, personal question. A listener calling out a suspicious performer carries a different weight than an artist calling out a peer.
26-year-old EDM producer Max “H4RRIS” Harris chose the latter. He calls out, on video, people he believes are passing off AI slop as human-made art.

“I don't see what AI produces as art, and I don't think this technology meaningfully advances art,” Harris says. “It's just a technological advance that hands people a way to steal real art and pass it off as their own.”

He described his own process much like any other creative medium: start from a core concept and throw out ideas until something clicks. His setup — Ableton Live, a Push 3, Serum, Kontakt — may look complicated, but he says it comes down to “me making the creative decisions.”

The tells come from the ear. Beyond vocals that all sound alike, there's a sharp hiss running through the whole track. His guess is that it comes from the model starting with a big blob of white noise and guessing at the waveform while referencing real song data.

What often gives away Suno-style tracks is a stutter: the vocal and other melodic elements cut off at the exact same instant. That happens because the model fails to properly separate the song's parts and treats them like one big instrument — a choice no producer would actually make.

He pointed to MANSA's “Midnight on My Mind” and Danny and Ian Asher's “Take Me (To The Moon)” as examples. None of the three has ever disclosed using a generative tool, though, and there's no conclusive proof. Harris could be wrong.

What pushed Harris to make his video was a Threads post about Suno from 39-year-old Italian producer Nihil Young. “It's like uploading an entire original track by an artist like Madonna and asking it to be remixed,” he said.

There was a cost. Young says he faced hacking attempts and online harassment, and even picked up fake followers inflating his Spotify numbers. The callouts have paused for now. Having mixed and mastered for Sony Music, Warner and Universal, he lost several clients as soon as AI spread.

The numbers point the other way. By Kapwing's estimate, the top 10 AI music creators on Spotify and YouTube made more than $6 million in 2025. Deezer has said more than half of new uploads are AI tracks, and Hallwood Media signed a $3 million deal with AI avatar Xania Monet.

“Put on a good pair of headphones and it's obvious the music was made by AI,” Young says. “But these days people consume music like fast food. They listen on phone speakers or play it in the background and don't pay attention to what it actually sounds like.”

blocks.cap: Photo Credit: Chris Bair

blocks.x: Spam farms have hijacked jazz musicians' YouTube and Spotify profiles. What pours out of them is generative AI tracks, with AI-rendered, anime-style female characters plastered on the cover art.

The Spotify, Amazon Music and YouTube profiles of jazz musicians, including William “Sonny” Criss, have been buried in AI spam to a worrying degree. Vocalist Jean Carne, cornetist Red Nichols and clarinetist Jimmie Noone have profiles in the same state. The “new songs” posted this year carry the publisher name “Ami bacuk.”

Two new songs appeared on Criss's Spotify profile — as Futurism put it, “an impressive feat for someone who died in 1977.” Both tracks have a generic anime-style female character on the cover, and the composer is listed as “Zainul Irpan,” which reads more like two common Arabic-origin names stuck together.

The songs are jazz-styled but nearly impossible to trace back to a source. Unlike typical AI slop, they're not remixes of Criss's own songs or of other artists' work that music-identification software would catch.

If tracks topped with modern anime characters hadn't suddenly flooded a deceased artist's profile, an ordinary listener would have had a hard time telling these songs apart from the musician's own work.
Back in April, the same publisher released four singles under Jimmie Noone's name. Noone was a Black Dixieland clarinetist and bandleader who died in 1944.

The titles are “You Have Hurt Him,” “You Have Hurt Him 2,” “He's still there” and “He's still there 2.” All are generic pop ballads with what sounds like an AI-sung female vocal. Even the surreal, AI corporate-Memphis-style header image clashes head-on with Noone's actual sound and his black-and-white photo album covers.

R&B and jazz vocalist Jean Carne (also spelled Carn)'s YouTube Music profile has also been overrun by slop. The signs are nearly identical to Criss's page, and the music is flat jazz missing Carne's trademark five-octave voice. There's one decisive difference: Carne is still alive.

A Spotify spokesperson told Futurism that “the releases in question have been removed from the artist profiles,” adding that “protecting artist identity is a top priority for us, and we continue to invest heavily in detection and prevention.”

Spotify also pointed to Artist Profile Protection, currently being tested in stages ahead of a full launch. It lets artists review and approve or reject incoming releases before they go live. Still, it remains an open question why this has to be opt-in rather than the default on streaming services — especially since the feature itself was prompted by profile hijackings on Spotify in the first place.

The upshot is that platforms are reacting after the fact rather than getting ahead of the flood of AI slop. When the public can't tell a track was made by AI, a service like Spotify has more to gain than to lose. That makes Deezer's choice to actively identify AI tracks and pull them from its royalty pool carry that much more weight.

blocks.cap: So pretty. Screenshot: Terrence O'Brien / The Verge

blocks.x: The piece starts with a memory of being obsessed with Spirograph as a kid. Those geometric patterns were hypnotic and beautiful. On top of that is a taste for generative music composition.
So when the two meet in a single browser tab, it's no surprise the writer got hooked.
The concept behind Musical Spirograph is fairly simple. A few points move around the screen following mathematical equations, tracing hypotrochoids and epitrochoids.
Every time those points cross a concentric ring, a specific note sounds. The drawing becomes the score.

That alone is fun enough, but there's plenty to tinker with. You can choose from six virtual rotors, and run up to three drawing arms at once. There are several parameters for shaping the pattern as well.
There are six scale options to pick from, or you can set the notes directly yourself. There are also six synth presets.
You can change the quantize setting and the BPM, or increase the number of rings up to two octaves.
There are weak points. The sound engine isn't great, and clipping and artifacts crop up easily. It's also a shame there's no MIDI output to control other instruments.
Even so, it's enough to get lost in for a good while. In the writer's own words, it's calm, hypnotic, and fun to fiddle with.

blocks.cap: The University of Alberta surveyed 263 Canadian musicians

blocks.x: The University of Alberta asked 263 “working Canadian musicians” what they're experiencing in a changing music industry. Optimism was rare when respondents talked about the industry's rapid technological shifts, especially generative AI.

Of the 142 who weighed in on AI's rapid spread, 87% viewed it “negatively.” A significant share said they don't use these tools in their own music at all, citing the way it drives down the value of human-made work. Others said bringing in new listeners and earning a livable income keep getting harder.

Beyond the moral issue the survey summed up as “a loss of human artistry,” musicians also pointed to copyright theft, environmental concerns, and “fears that AI-generated tracks could threaten their livelihoods by burying real music.”

The charts felt it too. The electronic duo HAVEN's viral EDM track “I Run” made the Billboard Canadian Hot 100. After it came out that the uncredited female vocal was made with the AI tool Suno, they replaced it with TikTok singer Kaitlin Aragon, and it's that version that charted.

Views on streaming are similarly twisted. The study describes artists as having a “forced ambivalent relationship” with these platforms. Succeeding in the digital era makes them a “practical necessity,” but that sits alongside low payouts and distrust of “opaque algorithms that have replaced organic discovery.” Many respondents said they'd like to leave but see no alternative.

“Musicians lived through the shift to streaming about a decade ago, and they still haven't recovered or seen the benefits of it,” said lead researcher Brian Fauteux. He added that artists now face “another variable in AI, coming out of the Big Tech world, from people who don't seem to see music as an art or a craft.”
“This isn't anger that came out of nowhere,” Fauteux said. “These issues go back to years of labels and exploitation, full of stories of musicians not getting paid properly or losing their rights.”

blocks.cap: Alibaba's booth at CES in Las Vegas, January 2019. Photo: David Becker/Getty Images

blocks.x: Chinese tech giant Alibaba launched its own AI music generation model this week. The company says it turns prompts like “millennial Mandopop” or “the feeling of dawn in urban folk” into finished songs. Prices start under $10.

It was built by Alibaba's Token Hub, an AI business unit launched in March that CEO Eddie Wu personally oversees. Happy Shrimp 1.0 partnered with TAIHE MUSIC GROUP, China's largest music label and an audio entertainment company. It's still in beta, but within the site you can make AI music, upload it, find and listen to it, and leave likes and comments. Membership starts at $14.90 a month, and credit packages start at $9.90.

Happy Shrimp joins Alibaba's Happy family of AI models, following Happy Horse, an AI video generation service, and Happy Oyster, which makes 3D interactive video for game developers. E-commerce businesses like AliExpress and Taobao remain the core of Alibaba's business, but the Happy models come out of Token Hub, the central AI research unit Wu set up to push more commercial AI models into the market.

“Our number one goal is to pursue [artificial general intelligence],” Wu said on an investor call in February 2025, according to Bloomberg. “We will continue to develop models that push the boundaries of intelligence.”

The past year in the music industry has been a tangle of three threads: AI music platforms competing for growth and capital, music companies trying to profit from and get inside whatever comes next, and a camp opposed to the pairing of technology and music itself. Suno, the largest AI music platform in the U.S., announced its second deal with a major music company, signing a licensing agreement with BMG after an earlier one with Warner Music Group. Spotify said it will label AI music starting in September and is rolling out an AI remix feature built with UMG, Merlin, and Kobalt.

The Happy Shrimp website describes the model this way: “It treats music as a language with its own grammar, meaning, and context. Instead of creating lyrics, melody, arrangement, and vocals separately and stitching them together, it designs them together, so the whole track comes out as one coherent song.”
Prompts can be long or short. You can use professional music terminology or write in internet slang. The site claims a finished track pops out in seconds.

Alibaba and strategic partner TAIHE are exploring further opportunities like “artist co-creation and high-quality content development,” according to Alizila, Alibaba's English-language corporate news site.

blocks.cap: Instagram First Draft

blocks.x: The moment they look at a pile of raw footage, a lot of musicians and creators just decide not to post it at all.

To push past that threshold, Instagram has launched First Draft. It's a one-tap editing feature that trims and stitches video clips together on its own, turning them into a single flowing Reel in seconds.

It's currently rolling out on iOS only. Think of it as a digital assistant that takes over the most tedious part of video editing, the “rough cut” stage. An Android version looks likely to follow soon.
First Draft is a native editing tool built just for Instagram Reels. It trims the clips you choose, strips out unnecessary pauses, and strings together the best moments into a first edit.
It mainly detects audio and motion to spot dead air and cut out those gaps. It doesn't rely on generative AI.

There are two ways to use it. Open the Reels gallery from your camera roll, pick one or more clips, and tap the “First Draft” button at the bottom of the screen, or shoot directly with the Instagram camera and tap “First Draft” to assemble the footage right away.
It doesn't care about format, from everyday vlogs to tour montages stitched from multiple clips to plain talking-head videos.

Any edit First Draft makes is 100% reversible. If you don't like the rhythm of the automatic edit, you can rearrange the clips, restore them, or discard everything, then move into the full editor to add music, text, and effects.
Short-form video is an inseparable part of music marketing today. But for independent musicians running their own campaigns, editing is a massive bottleneck.

By automating the most annoying, time-consuming part, cutting dead air and assembling a basic montage, Instagram hands artists back their time. With the rough-cut grunt work out of the way, they can spend it polishing the narrative, talking with fans, and actually making music. If you have an iPhone, that's one less excuse not to post a tour vlog or a track breakdown.

blocks.cap: Stable Audio early beta. Image: Stability AI

blocks.x: Everyone takes a different path to the soundscape, score or song they're after. Working methods vary too, and at the start you never know where an idea will end up going.
So there's no way you'd arrive there in one shot.
Stability AI said it held onto that point while thinking through the next stage of Stable Audio. The goal is simple: hand people a tool for shaping sound, not just spitting it out.

So it released two ways to work with Stable Audio 3.0 together: the Stable Audio plugin, which brings generation straight into the DAW, and an enhanced StableAudio.com web experience for refining what you've made. Both run on a commercially safe model, and the output belongs to the user and can be freely distributed.
Both are in beta. The company says some features are experimental and that it will keep refining the experience in real time.

blocks.cap: The Stable Audio plugin running directly on a DAW track. Image: Stability AI

blocks.x: The plugin generates audio directly on a DAW track. You can arrange, edit and process the sound right there, building it up alongside the rest of the session.
It works like an instrument. In Ableton it sits under PlugIns on an Instrument track; in Logic it loads into an Instrument slot.

It syncs to the session BPM, so it lands right in the tempo of whatever project you're working on. You also choose the length, from a short section to a full six-minute piece. Multiple takes can sit in a playlist for comparison before you decide what to keep.
Supported formats are macOS AU and VST3. It works on both Apple Silicon and Intel Macs, and is compatible with major DAWs including Logic Pro and Ableton Live.

blocks.cap: The new web app for continuing to refine a track in the browser. Image: Stability AI

blocks.x: The web app follows a musician's actual sequence: lay down an idea, listen to it, fix it, then run it again. The first take is generated from a prompt.

From there, you give direction in words — ask it to cut the low end, push the build back further, or change the instrumentation. With audio-to-audio, you can also pull different genres, moods and variations out of a sound you already have.

Working by part is also open now. You mix with level, pan, mute and solo, and apply per-track effects as well as master effects. Bounce just the parts you want and export the mix to keep working elsewhere.

If a take falls just short, there's no need to start all over again. What this beta is ultimately pitching is a session you can keep living in. The team added that it wants to hear from musicians, producers, composers, sound designers and audio developers about what helps and what gets in the way.

It's release week. The music is done, but the artist's work is just getting started. Checking the distributor, looking over streaming dashboards, setting up ads, tracking payouts. Assets and campaign notes are scattered across five or six apps, and audience data lives somewhere else entirely.

This isn't happening because the tools are bad. Most of them do their one job very well. That's exactly why the real problem is hard to see. Karan Dasgupta says what independent artists lack isn't a tool for planning release strategy, but a system that ties those tools together.

For years, music tech has split an artist's career into pieces and bolted software onto each problem. Distribution, smart links, ad buying, there's a specialized service for each one. It's clearly worked to remove gatekeepers and lower costs. But every new solution added one more login, one more dashboard, one more subscription. Each individual problem got solved, but nobody knows how the pieces fit together.

blocks.cap: Source: Hypebot

blocks.x: These days an independent artist is effectively running a company. Marketing, financial management, release planning, distribution, and branding all at once. One person does what a startup would split across a team. The technology that made independence possible quietly turns into an operating burden. Independence should mean owning your career, not spending it running software.

The real cost isn't the subscription fees, it's attention. To figure out why a release underperformed, streaming numbers, ad performance, social response, and revenue are scattered across different systems, and the artist has to stitch them together by hand. Switching between tasks and resetting your head each time creates more friction than the work itself. Weeks and months of that pile up into duplicated effort and missed opportunities.

So the question needs to change. Not which tool is best for this job, but how that tool connects to everything else. A good system doesn't just execute actions, it links them. A release feeds into a distribution schedule, that schedule feeds into a marketing campaign, the campaign feeds into audience data, and the data feeds into the next release decision. A layer where features talk to each other without one company replacing every specialized service, that's the difference between a toolkit and an operating system.

blocks.cap: UpNComer dashboard screen. Source: Hypebot

blocks.x: AI makes this picture matter more. AI gets used to pull out ideas and read data, but intelligence without context has limits. An AI that only knows one task gives you an answer. A system that knows releases, audience, and finances together explains why that answer matters. Dasgupta says the best AI is the AI an artist is least aware of, AI that sits underneath the workflow instead of becoming one more place to visit.

The first era of independent music tech was about access. The next is about connection. Past a certain point, more tools stop meaning freedom and start meaning another job. Over the next ten years, the companies that matter won't be the ones adding another dashboard, they'll be the ones taking dashboards away. What independent music lacked was never a tool. It was always a system.

blocks.cap: Search has moved from inferred intent to declared intent. Source: Digital Music News

blocks.x: Late at night, someone says this: play something wide and beautiful I haven't heard before. No vocals, piano is fine, but not too sentimental. No artist name, no song title, no genre. They just described a situation, and the machine picks the answer.

Michael Whelan reads this scene as the latest version of a gatekeeper swap. There were record store clerks, then radio programmers. MTV, magazines, and distributor buyers came next. The internet said it would remove gatekeepers, but it actually automated them. Search engines, social media, streaming, playlists, and recommendation systems each took that seat in turn.

What's changing this time is how intent gets read. Streaming algorithms watched behavior to infer intent. Predicting what comes next from what you skipped and what you saved made it a system that was always looking backward. Now you can just say it. Whelan sums it up as inferred intent shifting to declared intent.

Spotify has already gone deep into prompt playlists and conversational controls, and YouTube Music has been building natural-language discovery too. Amazon experimented with prompt-based playlist generation. People never thought in metadata fields to begin with. Nobody says give me mid-tempo neoclassical instrumental music between 70 and 82 BPM with low vocal probability. They just ask for something pretty to play while they eat.

Discovery moving outside music apps is also a big shift. If a conversation about travel or making dinner turns to music, the first point of contact happens inside a general-purpose AI. The Spotify search bar disappears. The song gets heard first, and the artist's name comes later. For unknown musicians, that's both an opportunity and a disaster.

Genre loses power too. A request for instrumental music to make an unfamiliar hotel room feel comfortable has no use for a genre name. Instead, the machine listens to the sound itself and pulls out tempo, instrumentation, texture, density, presence of vocals, harmony, and energy, then connects that to the person's words. Discovery depends less on whether tags were applied correctly. Old catalogs come back to life too. A song for running at a desert sunrise has no particular reason to have come out last Friday.

There are two things Whelan watches out for. One is the habit of making music to fit a prompt. If arrangements start getting optimized for sleep, focus, or running, AI hasn't discovered art, it has quietly placed an order. The other is an invisible gatekeeper. Nobody explains why those twenty songs got picked out of tens of millions. A radio DJ at least had a name.

So the practical task that remains isn't tag games. It's keeping descriptive information, mood, instrumentation, vocal presence, culture, tempo, credits, collaborators, accurate. It's also making sure your website and Spotify, Instagram, and Bandcamp don't say different things from each other. Discovery may get easier, but a song getting discovered doesn't mean you got discovered.

The Prime 4, released in 2019, is a 4-deck standalone DJ system that connects directly to TIDAL, SoundCloud Go+, Beatport, and Dropbox over Wi-Fi. It also has independent zone outputs and multiple storage and connectivity options. This G2 generation significantly boosts processing power and adds new performance features.

Because Denon DJ and AKAI Professional sit under the same InMusic umbrella, technology from the MPC G2 carried over to the Denon DJ line. The first thing that stands out is the 16-pad MPCe multi-zone performance pad. It reads velocity and pressure and even does 3D sensing, so hot cues, effects, rolls, stems, and DMX lighting control all layer onto a single pad.

blocks.cap: Prime 4 G2 top panel. Source: Denon DJ

blocks.x: Inside, it packs an 8-core ARM CPU and 4GB of RAM. Processing stems on the unit itself takes that much power. The 10.1-inch main touchscreen stays the same, but the jog wheel grew to 8 inches and now has an LED display attached.

It pulls stems straight from a track while DJing. There are dedicated buttons for creating instrumentals and acapellas, and Stem FX and Stem EQ also open from there. A 3-pin SoundSwitch output connects DMX lighting, supporting Philips Hue and Nanoleaf standards.

blocks.cap: Main panel. Source: Denon DJ

blocks.x: OmniSource switches seamlessly between USB, streaming, Serato DJ Pro, and VirtualDJ even during playback. The effects section also got bigger, and Amazon Music Unlimited and Apple Music streaming were added. The Prime 4 G2 is already on sale, with a street price of 2,698 euros.

Elastic Melody was already a favorite melody generator on Mac, iPad, and iPhone. It has a built-in synth engine inspired by the Dave Smith Evolver, and it can also send signal out to other apps or hardware. Now, with Pitch and Filter Drive modes added, it also works as a bassline maker and a percussion source.

Oliver Greschke keeps riding a good streak on the Elastic line. (Full disclosure: I worked on an early version of WretchUp and on a preset collection for Elastic OSC.) The built-in engine is one thing, but the ability to hand melodies off to other apps, including Elastic OSC, is what makes me want to dig back in.
Some of it unlocks via in-app purchase, but there's a lot you get just from the free update.

blocks.cap: Screenshot

blocks.x: Four more oscillator waveforms were added, along with pitch modulation. FM and FM decayed are additional purchases. The mixing screen was reworked too, adding a master level and volume meter, making solo/mute placement easier, and letting you rename tracks with a long press.

The Rnd shift knob is a clever idea. Every set number of repeats, the sequencer randomizes a note's pitch so the pattern keeps rolling, and tapping it twice brings back the original pattern. It's good both for adding variation and for pulling out acid lines.

Automation recording has also arrived — that's the big waveform you see in the screen above. FX sends were added, and EQ was moved to the end of the FX and dry chain. The new Ping Pong Delay and Datorro Reverb are additional purchases. Preset management and favorites got easier, and timing, performance when switching to Bluetooth headphones, buffer size switching, and macOS behavior all improved.

All of this lives inside a single app that also runs standalone and as an AUv3 plugin on both desktop and mobile. With fast randomization, Ableton Link support, and a song mode, it covers most of what you'd need.
To mark this release, SOI and Another Machines each put out presets. The Another Machines set leans toward heavy techno.

The shadow of the DFAM shows up again. Moog proved that modulating steps and layering on noise is enough to turn a sequencing synth into percussion. Here, pitch modulation, FM, and a new filter type carry that idea forward in Elastic's own way.

Elastic Melody can be used as a sequencer for pretty much anything, including Elastic OSC. Oliver just wrote in to say, 「Elastic OSC is clean, precise, digital, and Elastic Melody is warm, messy, growly analog.」 That sounds about right. It's nice to get to use both together.
Take a look at the walkthrough video below. Even if the early sounds seem flat, keep watching and listening — that's actually the point. Things can head in a very different direction.

This connects directly to something Mad Mike said in yesterday's archive interview. Pick up someone's old iPhone or iPad for two or three hundred dollars, or inherit one, make techno with this app, and someone will think it's a modular system. That's not a call to all get trapped together in a consumer-electronics upgrade cycle that chews up the planet. It's just worth seeing how much headroom is sitting dormant inside that silicon.

Adam Crute, who has used Cubase since its first version in 1989, picked up Logic Pro 12.3 again. The resentment built up from wrestling with Logic back in the Emagic days lingered for a long time, but today's product is different from that era. Opening it up, the first thing he noticed was how similar the two DAWs are. Track headers and content layout are alike, and so is the side-and-bottom panel structure for pulling out the inspector, browser, and mixer.

blocks.cap: Legacy Logic plugins left over as a remnant of skeuomorphic design. Image: Press

blocks.x: There are complaints too. Logic lumps the separate concepts of folder tracks and group tracks into a single Stack Tracks, which is confusing. It demands a key signature every time you start a project, and aux tracks only appear once you add a send. Output levels on the bundled instrument plugins run too hot, and there are far too many legacy plugins that are hard on the eyes. The lack of a tool to match Cubase's drum editor, forcing drums to be entered on the piano roll, is a longstanding frustration too.

blocks.cap: Project key signature settings in Logic Pro 12.3. Image: Press

blocks.x: Even so, there's quite a lot to like. Live Loops, with its non-linear pattern sequencing, meshes with the timeline far more smoothly than Cubase's Groove Agent SE. Session Players reads a project's chord progression and rhythm to generate convincing bass, drum, and keyboard parts, and Cubase's pattern players don't come close. Stem separation stood alongside, or above, the best he's experienced.

blocks.cap: Session Players in Logic Pro 12.3. Image: Press

blocks.x: The changes in 12.3 itself don't take long to list. Beat Breaker can now apply filter, resonance, and pan per slice and randomize them, loop detection improved, and Flex was paired with Smart Tempo. Chord ID, which catches chords, got faster and more accurate. Alchemy and Sample Alchemy gained a Sync mode that adjusts grain formant and overlaps parallel grain streams.

The rating is 8 out of 10. Even if the update looks thin, it's free for existing users, and the £199 price is less than half of Cubase Pro. Factor in more than 50GB of content, and the value is hard to argue with. The conclusion: Cubase remains the main tool, but Logic looks set to get pulled out often too.

Lucinate, from the team behind the much-loved iPad app AUM, is a real-time visual environment for macOS and iOS built on Apple's Metal technology. You can treat it as a ready-to-play video synth that supports Ableton Link and Link Audio. If you want to dig into shaders or build your own, you can move into live coding.

This is a tool worth waiting for. Good visual synths already exist. If you're collecting iPad visual synths, Imaginando's VS and Chromatose are genuinely beautiful. The same goes for editing shaders live: Hexler's KodeLife, which crosses OpenGL, DirectX, and Metal, sits on the text-coding side, and the free node-based app MetalGraph has also newly arrived on iPad and Mac. The problem comes after you've been tinkering with a shader — you eventually have to move to a different environment.

What makes Kymatica's Lucinate welcome is that it fits all of that into one environment. It's good for light play synced via Ableton Link, and now, with Link Audio, hooking sound to visuals is also quick. If the mood strikes, you can then dig into shader code live or build one from scratch and learn as you go. Since we're in the age of vibe coding, it's worth adding that poking around without fully knowing what you're doing is genuinely fun.

Looking through the specs, each one makes sense. It's a universal app spanning Mac, iPad, and iPhone, and it sits on Apple Metal. Being layer-based, it allows free blending and modular composition, and it comes with parametric shaders such as image correction, effects, texture utilities, coordinate transforms, patterns and gradients, and shader art examples. A built-in editor and an extensive Metal Shading Language library let you inspect, edit, and write shaders yourself.

For input, it uses a live camera plus imported images and video clips. Output can be recorded as video or pulled as stills. Any parameter can be modulated with MIDI, LFOs, or an audio analyzer, and synced to the beat via Ableton Link or MIDI Clock. Sound from other apps comes in through Ableton Link Audio, and external displays and projectors are also supported.

Put alongside VS, Chromatose, and KodeLife, a decent iPad, or even an iPhone, becomes a solid piece of visual gear. Grab a single HDMI adapter and this rig is ready to go. Or just run it on the same Mac. These days, even a fairly modest Apple Silicon machine can handle this comfortably. The Apple platform has quietly become a video-synth lab.
A camera, a few shaders, and synchronization alone already make this a pretty big tool.
As you can see, they've even built a genuinely usable UI for iPhone.
$29.99 on the App Store. It may be the best money spent in live visuals right now, especially alongside fun things like Quantum VJ HD from the SunVox developer.

Brazilian DJ and producer Alok teamed up with the agency Rise New York & Partners to run a campaign for his headphone line, WAAW by Alok. Buying the headphones gets you a music video made just for you. The premise was that a human holds the creative key.

blocks.cap: WAAW by Alok campaign

blocks.x: The starting point was ordinary. An official video set to Alok's track was shot first, with its visual texture drawn from the pop-art style of Brazilian illustrator Rogério Puhl. An engine was layered on top of that.

Gemini Omni acts as the brain managing the flow of video, sound design, and text adaptation. The Google Maps API reads the fan's surroundings to work real landmarks into the story, and the Google Weather API matches lighting and weather to that place on that day. Style trends are tracked through YouTube and Trends data, and the actual video clips are produced by Vertex AI and Veo. The rendering pipeline runs on Google Cloud.
Fans submit a Beat Profile carrying their tastes and real-time environmental data. In return, they get a video with their own neighborhood's weather and city skyline worked into the background.

Control was kept through rules. The team spent weeks testing the engine against five visual rules, discarding 81.4 percent of the draft clips produced along the way. Camera movement, color, and the story's key beats stayed locked, with only designated sections left open.

Muse Group has released Audacity 4. The company calls it the biggest update in its 25-year history. Clip editing was rebuilt from the ground up, and the interface got reworked too. The ties to audio.com run tighter now. The price is still $0.

blocks.cap: Audacity 4

blocks.x: Clips can now overlap. You can select and edit multiple clips at once, or group them to move as one. Everything is non-destructive, so trimmed audio comes back if you stretch the clip out again. How the audio behind a deleted section fills the gap is set through the ripple editing option.

The Split tool, long requested by the community, is here. It cuts one track or several at once, right at the playhead. Clip envelopes bring volume automation inside the clip itself, letting you draw fades without touching the original recording. Built-in effects got a visual redesign only; what they do hasn't changed. Real-time effects and VST3, Audio Unit, and LV2 support are still there.

A home screen exists for the first time. It shows local projects and cloud projects stored on audio.com in one place, laid out as thumbnails instead of file names so they're easier to scan. Workspaces save a separate screen layout for each kind of task, so switching from podcast editing to music work no longer means resetting the whole app.

blocks.cap: The redesigned interface

blocks.x: The look changed more than at any point in its history, as Muse Group put it. Toolbars and track controls were rearranged, and the playback and recording meters were swapped out. The playhead stays visible at all times, and panning and zooming feel smoother. Light and dark themes, an accent color picker, and a reworked high-contrast mode come along with it.

blocks.cap: The cleaned-up toolbar and track controls

blocks.x: Muse Group Chief Product Officer Julia Sazhina said Audacity has helped creators record and edit for more than 25 years, and that version 4 is meant to carry it through the next 25—while leaving what people already loved about it untouched.

AI tools stay in place. A bundle of Intel OpenVINO-based plugins handles stem separation, music generation, transcription using Whisper.cpp, and noise suppression. They run on the PC itself without uploading audio to a server. Version 4 remains free and open source, and the official release is available from MuseHub.
Armin van Buuren and Laidback Luke have joined Moises as the first artists in its artist partnership program.

blocks.cap: Armin van Buuren and Laidback Luke

blocks.x: Moises positions itself as an alternative to platforms like Suno, claiming it trains its models only on licensed, authorized tracks and files. Ableton, Fender, the Whitney Houston Foundation, Cory Henry, Jordan Rudess, and Berklee Online are already tied to the company, and Charlie Puth joined as Chief Music Officer earlier this year.

The two musicians' role is to give feedback on its DJ and production tools. They're also helping refine the studio tool suite, which includes stem separation, isolation, chord recognition, and mastering.

Founder and CEO Geraldo Ramos said, “The next generation of creative tools needs to be built with musicians, not for them.” Laidback Luke added that a good tool doesn't work for you instead—it helps you listen better, learn faster, and make sharper calls. Van Buuren set one condition: whether the artist holds the control.

The platform, which started in dance music, is broadening its genres. It's now used by roughly 80 million people across 190 countries, with the U.S., Brazil, India, France, and Japan as its biggest markets.

The backdrop is messy. By SubmitHub's count, nearly 40 percent of tracks released in July had AI involved somewhere, and a third of the artists categorized that way denied using it. Last month, Beatport banned fully AI-generated tracks outright. After Sony Music took down 135,000 deepfake songs in March, Traxsource, Bandcamp, and Deezer followed similar paths.
Producely Dialr, first shown at Superbooth25, is finally taking orders. It is a plugin controller.

blocks.cap: Producely Dialr

blocks.x: It comes from Producely, a startup in Copenhagen, Denmark, founded by Morten Søderquist Li, who worked in music technology.

Plugin controllers already exist from SSL and Softube. What sets Dialr apart is automatic mapping. It scans your installed VST3 and AU plugin library and sends the parameter data to Producely's AI cloud, which builds a controller profile for that combination and sends it back. Once received, it works offline.

A 7-inch LCD touchscreen shows parameter names and values, and reassigns the layout each time you switch plugins or pages. The knobs sit in two rows of six, in three sizes, so your hand learns their positions. Step encoders on either side of the screen page through plugin sections, fine-tune values, and move between DAW tracks.

blocks.cap: 12 knobs and a 7-inch touchscreen
Rear view

blocks.x: Its range is broad, covering everyday audio processors, soft synths, and control plugins that run WesAudio and Bettermaker hardware. The bet is that you won't have to remap from scratch every time you add a plugin.
It is now taking pre-orders, with shipping starting within weeks.
This video covers how to build your own audio effects using Studio Chat in Suno Studio 2.0. It is hosted by Henry Fipps.

Two things get built: a stereo doubler and a pitch-shifting delay. You type the effect you want into the chat, the AI proposes a build plan first, and once you confirm and save it, it lands in My Plugins.

After loading the finished stereo doubler onto a track to check the sound, a new plugin called Crystal Sparkle is built and placed on a drum track. The video closes by noting plugin features coming next.
The tool that once wrote your song now also builds the processors that refine it. Suno filmed the 5-minute-55-second walkthrough itself.

Two years after winning an Engineering, Science & Technology Emmy for dxRevive Pro, Accentize has been named again, this time for its reverb-matching plugin Chameleon.
