The award is given by the Television Academy in Los Angeles and honors engineering, science and technology achievements that have had a major impact on the television industry.

blocks.cap: Accentize Chameleon reverb-matching plugin

blocks.x: Accentize says Chameleon was built to address a long-standing headache in audio post-production: matching the acoustic character of recordings made in different environments. Newly recorded material such as ADR, dubbing and Foley needs to sit naturally within the production sound, but if the room reverb differs, the result still feels disconnected no matter how well the original was captured.

Chameleon analyzes the reverb characteristics of a reference recording and generates a reverb profile to apply to other tracks. Dialogue mixers and others can quickly recreate a location's acoustic color without rebuilding it by hand.

Benjamin Graf, founder of Accentize and developer of Chameleon, said: “Winning an Emmy for dxRevive Pro in 2024 was already beyond anything we imagined. Getting this kind of recognition again with Chameleon is truly special. The two products address different problems in dialogue post-production, but they started from the same motivation: using new technology to make difficult, time-consuming audio work easier for professionals. We're deeply grateful to the audio community that helped grow these tools with their feedback and support.”
The award will be presented at the Engineering, Science & Technology Emmy Awards ceremony on Wednesday, October 14, at the Television Academy's Saban Media Center in Los Angeles.
Dreamtonics, the Tokyo company behind the vocal synthesis tools Synthesizer V and Vocoflex, has released Instrument X. It marks the company's move from vocal synthesis into orchestral scoring.

blocks.cap: Dreamtonics Instrument X

blocks.x: Rather than relying on a multi-gigabyte sample library, Instrument X turns sheet music directly into sound using neural acoustic modeling. Instead of static loop triggers, composers and producers control bowing, breath and key articulation themselves.

The engine runs up to eleven simultaneous microphone feeds, including close mics, a Decca tree and room ambience. To keep the channels aligned, Dreamtonics developed — and has filed a patent for — a method that measures a studio's acoustic geometry using a custom dodecahedral speaker array. A physics-augmented neural network separates the room's directional acoustics from the dry instrument source. It needs no internet connection and no dedicated GPU, running locally on an ordinary laptop.

Key features include an articulation editor that combines automatic Smart Articulation with manual, note-by-note control, letting staccato, legato, col legno and mute be layered on a single note. The dynamics lane automatically draws context-appropriate dynamics while also shifting the instrument's timbre and overtones, with manual override available. AI performance retakes let users regenerate an entire phrase or adjust just the timbre drift, micro pitch curve or motion intensity. Overlapping notes render as fully independent voices, and a mic mixer panel balances spot mics, the Decca tree and the room.

The launch lineup spans three collections and fifteen instrument expansions. Strings: Violin 1, Viola 1, Violoncello 1, Contrabass 1. Woodwinds: Flute 1, Piccolo 1, Oboe 1, Clarinet in A 1, Bassoon 1. Brass: Trumpet 1, Trombone 1, Horn 1, Tuba 1. Each instrument comes with five style presets — Adagio, Allegro, con Fuoco, Pop and Ballade — that change the entire emotional color of a performance.

Founder and CEO Kanru Hua said the company considered folding the instruments into its existing workspace but ultimately chose a separate platform. “Many users had asked us to bring the instruments into our ecosystem. Rather than overloading a single workspace, we decided to build Instrument X as a standalone platform alongside Synthesizer V and Vocoflex, completing a trilogy.” He added that matching professional composition and production standards was harder than the AI synthesis itself, and that the engine had to be rebuilt from the ground up to reflect the physics of each instrument family — though the workflow remains familiar to existing Synthesizer V users.

It is sold through the Dreamtonics Store. The core editor is free with the purchase of any expansion pack. A 14-day editor trial and a 7-day instrument trial can be activated directly from the Product Manager panel. Individual expansion packs cost $99, the Orchestral Strings collection $249, Orchestral Woodwinds $279, Orchestral Brass $249, pick-and-mix packs range from $158 to $396, and the Orchestral Essentials bundle is $349.

SOCAN, the Canadian music rights organization, has sued the AI music platform Suno for copyright infringement. It alleges that the Suno service generates and streams unauthorized copies of songs in SOCAN's repertoire.

blocks.cap: SOCAN and Suno

blocks.x: The complaint was filed on September 2 in Canada's Federal Court. According to Music Business Worldwide, it identifies 150 Suno-generated tracks drawn from 137 songs represented by SOCAN. At issue are both the outputs and the streaming of them to Canadian users.

The songs named include Avril Lavigne's “Sk8er Boi,” Tom Cochrane's “Life Is a Highway” and Joni Mitchell's “Both Sides Now.” SOCAN also posted comparison material online that lets listeners play the original recordings alongside the Suno tracks it alleges infringe them.

blocks.cap: Screenshot of SOCAN's AI lawsuit page

blocks.x: Andrea Kokonis, SOCAN's Chief Legal Officer and General Counsel, told Billboard Canada that Suno entered Canada in December 2023 without SOCAN's consent, and that subsequent discussions had not resolved the dispute. “We want to make sure that when our members' songs are used, the value flows back to our members.”

SOCAN sought damages and profits arising from the infringement, or alternatively statutory damages of CA$20,000 per song. It also requested CA$10 million in punitive and exemplary damages, along with a court order to prevent further infringement. Neither report carried a response from Suno to the lawsuit.

The startup Songscription first came into view in July 2025, when TechCrunch covered its 'automatic music transcription' service. The copyright 'gray area' question came up at the same time. That November, the company raised $5 million, and advisor and music-tech veteran Elizabeth Moody publicly said it would sign deals with publishers and take an ethical approach. This month we spoke with CEO Andrew Carlins about how that arrangement works and how AI is used in transcription and arrangement.

blocks.cap: Songscription's automatic sheet-music transcription screen

blocks.x: At the time of the funding round, users had surpassed 150,000. Carlins says growth has since exceeded 20% a month, and most new users are "singer-songwriters and creators transcribing their own work into sheet music for the first time." Features have kept being added: chord recognition, a feature that simplifies transcriptions "to match a player's level, including beginners," and a text-based notation editor with an AI chat interface. Aligning lyrics with music and generating lead sheets or duet arrangements from transcriptions are still in beta.

Deals with indie publishers are also continuing. So far only Spirit Music Group has been announced, but more are expected within weeks. "Publishers have generally been very supportive," Carlins says. "More than 90% of songs written today remain untranscribed, and even transcribed songs are limited in instrumentation and difficulty level. Publishers understand that Songscription can support artists' and songwriters' creative workflows and expand sheet-music access to players at every level."

He also said publishers value the fact that Songscription sought out license deals on its own initiative. "They seem more willing to license to us than to some other AI services." "Choosing to work with the industry early on wasn't a hard decision. If your mission is to empower artists and music learners, you know you have to work alongside the industry."

The company is also looking beyond its first service. It recently released Anything Piano, a piano-learning app for Apple devices, built on the observation that many Songscription users are "learning piano or looking for a more structured way to practice." "Anything Piano, in its current form, turns any audio into a simplified piano tutorial with guided fingering, and listens to a user playing piano to give feedback on their performance." The company recently renamed itself Play Anything, reflecting a broader mission of helping people learn and play songs they love. Songscription will be grown as a platform for creators and songwriters, while Anything Piano will be grown as a platform for learners and those seeking performance feedback.

blocks.cap: Australia's ARIA joined the global trend by excluding AI-generated songs from its charts. Source: ARIA

blocks.x: The landscape of Australia's music charts changed this week. The Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) decided to exclude songs made entirely by AI from its official charts. The trigger was an AI cover of Madonna's 'Like a Prayer' that had stayed in the top 20 for months. Australia is not acting alone. Under common principles set by the IFPI, more than 20 official charts, including those in the US and Europe, have already adopted similar rules.

The incident started with Australian DJ and producer Josh Fawaz. His AI-assisted Madonna cover got heavy radio rotation and climbed to No. 2 on the ARIA overall chart and No. 4 on the Top 20 Singles chart. Only after a strong industry backlash did Fawaz belatedly credit the vocals and drums as AI-made on Spotify, by which point streams had already passed 48 million.

As of Friday, August 28, tracks made entirely by AI lose their eligibility for ARIA charts. ARIA CEO Annabelle Herd said, “Music made wholesale by a service trained on other artists' recordings is fundamentally different from an artist using AI as a creative tool.” Going forward, charting requires human involvement in songwriting, lead vocals and key instrumentation, while AI playing a supporting role is allowed as long as there is no streaming or chart manipulation.

ARIA's new policy is built on common principles that the IFPI set last July together with several international music organizations. According to the IFPI, such AI chart policies are already in place at more than 20 official chart programs worldwide, making Australia's decision more an extension of an existing trend than an exception. GfK Entertainment, which runs the charts on behalf of Germany's BVMI, also quietly adopted similar principles in late July, weeks before Australia's announcement.

Charting does not require avoiding tools like Suno or Udio altogether. Using AI for sound design, arrangement ideas or as a starting point for inspiration is not a problem anywhere. But it is a different matter if vocals or key instrumental parts were generated wholesale without a human performance. Because the standard for what counts as “substantially human-made” is still loose, enforcing this rule in practice is likely to produce no shortage of ambiguous cases and disputes.

Billboard reaffirmed its commitment to accurately reflect global music consumption. For nearly 100 years, the Billboard charts have continued to evolve alongside the new modes of expression and technological change that music fans embrace.

Billboard said that classifying AI-made content requires both transparent disclosure from artists and creators and reliable tools to identify AI-generated music. It explained that this kind of collective effort to responsibly disclose AI use is needed for the charts to continue to capture music consumption accurately and responsibly.

Silvio Pietroluongo, Executive Vice President of Charts and Data Partnerships, said, “Achieving transparency around AI-generated music requires collaboration across the entire industry, from artists and labels to streaming services, technology companies and trade organizations.” He added, “We are glad to see the identification tools that are emerging continue to develop, and we will keep testing and using solutions from across the ecosystem going forward.”

Leila Cobo, Co-Head of Content, said, “Billboard has always championed artists, celebrated music and maintained editorial transparency.” She added, “In a time of change like this, creators who use AI need to disclose that use so that we, too, can be transparent and accurate in our editorial coverage and charts.”

Jason Lipshutz, Co-Head of Content, added, “The way AI is involved in contemporary music is changing by the day, but we will keep working, now and going forward, with industry stakeholders to make clear, well-grounded judgments.”

Billboard said it views new tools and efforts to tag and identify AI-generated songs favorably, including the AI detection program Luminate recently announced, and plans to broadly cooperate with related efforts by trade organizations and streaming services.

blocks.cap: Example screen of AI features built into FL Studio

blocks.x: Robert Linke, Chief Product and Technology Officer at Image-Line, said generative AI music tools can be a powerful onramp that draws even complete beginners into the world of making music themselves. The remarks came from the head of the company behind FL Studio, formerly known as FruityLoops.
Linke said in an interview on the Musically Focus podcast, “AI lets a lot more people around the world engage with music in a more creative way.”

“These days you can just type an idea into a prompt. It might not be the most creative output you've ever made, but it could be the first time that person has ever made a song themselves... and that experience pulls a lot of people further in,” he explained.

He added, “Once people realize, 'this is as far as I can go here, this is as far as I can interact with a generative platform,' they move on to the next step and download something like FL Studio to actually start making music.”
Linke called this “the net benefit of generative AI,” saying it means “a lot more people come to see their relationship with music as something they can creatively participate in.”

FL Studio has added AI features for several years, but Linke said there is a clear line in that process. “Any model we attach to FL Studio has to be ethically trained. We can't use a model trained on data where the rights holders weren't compensated. That's a really important principle,” he said.

“It also has to be better than the traditional way of doing things. Using AI just because it's AI doesn't make sense, because it's costly and technically heavy. So it needs to actually help people accomplish and achieve something that was hard to do before,” he said.

Linke and Image-Line CEO Constantin Köhncke also discussed, across the full podcast episode, the contradiction between how musicians talk about AI publicly and how they actually use it, and why text prompts are “not an ideal way to get into making music.”

blocks.cap: Lyria 3.5, Google's newly released music generation model

blocks.x: Google has released Lyria 3.5, which it calls its top-tier music generation model, in the Gemini app and the Gemini API. Refinements to vocal expression and arrangement allow for more polished tracks.

In the Gemini app, users can pick a genre directly or specify one through a description, and can choose between vocal and instrumental tracks. New templates were added for quickly starting anything from background music to birthday songs, and track length can be adjusted shorter or longer.
Whether it's background music for a video, a brand jingle or a personal ringtone, it has become much easier to bring an idea to life.

Lyria 3.5 is open to all users worldwide through web and mobile apps. Artists and AI creators can use the model in Google Flow Music, while developers and engineers can also access it in Google AI Studio and Google Vids.

This is written by Brad Stewart, founder of Music Mogul AI and Mogul Talent Group. His premise: the future of the music industry is not humans versus machines, but building a career by automating the work that was never worth your time in the first place.

Over more than 20 years of watching this industry, he says the people who built lasting careers were not the most talented. They were the most organized, or the ones who found a team that was. They answered emails and followed up. Meanwhile, the more talented artist next to them waited to be discovered and quietly disappeared.

This is the hidden cruelty of the independent era. The internet handed everyone the label's tools, and loaded the label's workload on top. We called that freedom. In practice, it often meant doing three things poorly alone at one in the morning instead of doing one thing well.

So the question is not whether AI should be allowed into music. It is already in, and it is not leaving. The remaining question is what to have it do. Aim it at the wrong things and you get soulless songs and empty marketing. Aim it right and you get back time, the resource this industry is always short on.

First, follow-up. What separates artists who keep booking shows from those who don't is not talent, it is follow-up. Who you emailed, what you said back, what you promised, remembered and acted on every week. Done by hand, it is a part-time job, and the first thing to collapse the moment things get busy.

This is where AI earns its place. It drafts messages, gathers venues, contacts and conversations in one spot, and surfaces the thread again before it goes cold. What it cannot do is close. Reading the room, naming a price, deciding whose car to drive, that stays human.

Second, content. No one needs reminding that artists have to keep posting. What's missing is the time to do it well and consistently at once. Step off stage at one in the morning and the algorithm still wants three posts this week.

In the repetitive middle stretch, AI is fairly capable. It turns one idea into a week's worth of captions, cuts one video into twelve clips, drafts the copy for a mailing list, and schedules it all to post overnight. What it should not do is stand in for voice, taste or narrative. No one has ever fallen for an artist who sounds like software.

Third, paperwork and pipeline. Contact lists, performance history, offer sheets, invoices, who still owes what. The least romantic use case, and in the writer's view the most valuable one. It keeps the data clean, drafts contracts and invoices, and flags deposits that never came in. Making the call and signing the deal still falls to a person.

Some things clearly do not change. If AI carries the repetitive infrastructure, agents, managers and publicists go back to judgment, taste and relationships. A machine does not earn a promoter's trust, and it cannot hear what is missing from a song.
So the advice is one thing: don't try to automate everything at once. Hand the machine the one task that drains you most first. Then spend the time you get back on the things only a person can do.
Roland released Melody Flip on September 4. It's an AI melody-generation tool for producers working in a DAW, which the company calls a “music creation partner.”
It was built together with Sony Computer Science Laboratories, the result of an ongoing research partnership between the two companies on music analysis technology.

It is not a tool that automatically spits out finished songs. Roland calls it a starting point, meant to help you find ideas, pick what matches your sense of things, and grow that into your own work. The target is the hardest part of making music: finding the first spark.

Output is grouped into units Roland calls Palettes. Each Palette contains four interlinked parts: melody, chords, bass and drums. The release version ships with about 250 palettes spanning various genres and styles.

There are two ways to start. Load an audio file, whether a track, loop or beat, and it analyzes structure, tempo, beat position, key, chord progression, genre and mood to recommend a matching palette. Or browse the library yourself and pick something close to the style you want.

Roland says it does not copy the melody of a loaded song outright. It uses its analysis methodology and reference points to propose a new direction instead. You listen to the result, try variations, tweak it, then export. Song analysis draws on Sony CSL's Music Information Retrieval research.

Export works for both audio and MIDI. Melody comes out with chord, bass and drum backing included, so you can bring it straight into a major DAW to keep editing and arranging. The company says this supports a workflow from sketches and demos through to finished productions.

It supports macOS and Windows. It runs as VST3 and AU on macOS 14, 15 and 26, and Windows 11, and is downloaded through Roland Cloud Manager 3.1.23 or later. It is included in every Roland Cloud membership, including the free tier.

It was first announced on March 17. At the time, Roland said a free trial would open in May, and stated that AI tools should amplify artists rather than replace them, with human intention, taste and creativity staying at the center while technology stands as a partner or co-creator.
Roland CEO Masahiro Minowa said Melody Flip marks a meaningful step forward for responsibly developed AI. Roland is also a founding supporter of The Principles for Music Creation with AI.
A comment from artist Ginnojo Hoshi in the launch materials captures its character well: among the many AI tools that deliver a finished product, Melody Flip leaves the final expression to the user.
Melody Flip is available now through Roland Cloud Manager.

You wake up in the morning and Mary J. Blige is in an ad for the AI music platform Suno. That alone would be surprising enough, but then you learn the campaign has already been pulled, and the reason is that she never approved it. Your eyes pop out, like an old Tex Avery cartoon character.
Variety reported it. The video in question was originally posted on Suno's Facebook page.
In the video, Blige watches a producer build a track with Suno in a recording studio. She offers a few suggestions and says the result is impressive.
Once the clip spread, online backlash was the expected next step. What was actually unexpected came after that: Suno pulled the ad and stated exactly why.

“Ms. Blige is an icon we all deeply admire. Since she emerged with works like ‘What's the 411,’ ‘No More Drama,’ ‘The Breakthrough,’ and ‘Growing Pains,’ she has never stopped innovating. That's why we wanted to work with her,” a Suno spokesperson told Variety.

The key part is the explanation that follows. “We entered into a business agreement with someone who represented themselves as Ms. Blige's official representative. As soon as we learned that was not true, and that Ms. Blige was uncomfortable, we ended the ad campaign.”
Questions remain. Quite a lot of them.
The clip itself is not fake. At some point, Blige really did sit in a studio and watch Suno, and gave her opinion on camera.
How someone who was not her official representative managed to set that up is a detail that will likely come out later.

Yamaha Creator Pass, unveiled in beta at SXSW in March, is effectively the company's first real software push. A company that has spent close to a century building the physical reality of instruments, from the DX7 and Montage to generations of pianos, PA systems and mixing consoles, has shipped a subscription platform.

First, a caveat. There is nothing inside the box that Yamaha built itself. No in-house DAW, no in-house plugin engine. What Yamaha built is the front door: a single login, a single bill, a curated passage leading to almost every tool you'd need.

Two years ago, the subscription services Attack covered were FL Cloud, Splice, Loopcloud, Tracklib and Beatport Studio. All five were essentially sample-and-plugin subscriptions at heart, and even Beatport Studio stops at ten plugins and sound packs.

Creator Pass is a different animal. It tries to cover the entire pipeline, creation, mastering, recording, distribution, promotion and podcasting, with more than 20 partner services. It fits best for someone just starting out in music, maybe a songwriter.

The pricing has been cleaned up once already. A structure that once ran seven tiers, from Beginner to Podcaster Complete, is now down to three: Starter ($9.99/month), Growth ($19.99/month) and Pro ($39.99/month). Podcaster Pass remains a standalone add-on at $29/month.

Every tier is built on the same four partners: Output for samples and instruments, LANDR for AI mastering and royalty-free loops and one-shots, Riverside for podcast recording, and Groover for pushing finished tracks to curators and playlists.

Starter is a songwriting-and-beat tool aimed at people who've never opened a DAW. Growth becomes genuinely useful once it adds Output Arcade, LANDR samples, a DAW bundle, AI mastering, more than 200 tutorial lessons, and four Groover pitch credits a month. Pro adds Output's deeper tools and ten credits.

The heaviest recent addition is the DAW. Growth and Pro subscribers get Cubase 15 AI, and annual subscribers at either tier get Ableton Live 12 Lite as well. It's free if you don't already have a DAW. Since Yamaha owns Steinberg outright, this is the card closest to being entirely its own.
Some things are discounts, not inclusions. Steinberg products beyond Cubase, Adobe, SoundCloud and DistroKid are all separate. You pay for them yourself, just at a lower rate.

The math is worth running. Buy LANDR mastering, a Riverside recording plan, an Output sample subscription and Groover credits separately, and you'll clear Growth's $19.99 before you've even touched a DAW.

For experienced producers, on the other hand, it mostly doesn't fit. It's a curated approach, not unlimited access to the top tier of each tool, and Groover credits are metered too. If you already have a mastering chain, a DAW and a distributor, this solves a problem you don't have.

It's smart and reasonably priced, but it still shows signs of being assembled. For someone starting completely from zero, Growth makes the most sense, since you don't have to stack twenty subscriptions before finishing your first song.

Once it became known that Olivia Rodrigo filled her new album's lyric videos with human-drawn art and animation, the news spread across social media within days. A single production decision became news.
It didn't stop there. She also launched a collection with Etsy bundling merchandise from independent women artists, adding a fan experience on top.
The same pattern shows up across the industry. Venues have started refusing AI-made flyer art, and YouTube, Substack and LinkedIn have all said they want to cut down on AI slop.

How many different roles this industry actually rests on usually isn't visible. Subtitlers who translate lyrics into other languages, animators who draw lyric videos frame by frame, session musicians who add strings remotely for artists they've never met face to face, and topliners who write melodies over someone else's beat.

Tal Gonen of Fiverr, who wrote the piece, points to platform demand data. Topline composition requests rose 466% and strings rose 116%. Because people are being called in rather than handing creation over entirely, composing rose 426% as well.

Behind the numbers are real jobs. Andrea Sacchi added Spanish subtitles to Ed Sheeran's YouTube channel and official videos. Grammy-nominated engineer Bo Vallis earned $1 million working with Pharrell and Lil Wayne through Fiverr.

The pattern holds outside music too. Searches for “AI content humanize” — requests to rewrite chatbot scripts, marketing emails and web copy to sound human-written — rose 641% over the past six months.
Gonen's advice is simple: budget for human collaborators the same way you would for a producer or a venue. Treat “handmade” itself as a marketing asset, not just an invisible production decision.
Crash United has released klattsch. It's a retro vocal synthesizer for desktop and Android, built on the design lineage that produced DECtalk and the machine voices of that era.
It isn't simply a clone of a familiar speech synthesizer. It reimplements the 1980 formant synthesizer prototype that had survived only in an MIT lab — the actual starting point of this lineage.

The developer dug into the proof-of-concept design left behind by Dr. Dennis Klatt — the very root that later became Stephen Hawking's voice. Not stopping there, they added three more speech synthesis engines, following papers from decades ago.

Not a single sample is used. It combines oscillators, noise and resonators within what was technically possible in 1980. The sound is crackly and unmistakably artificial, with every synthesis parameter exposed.

You can type text or draw notes on a piano roll, attach phonemes in English or Japanese kana, and hand-draw pitch curves. Multiple voice layers can be stacked across different engines. It can also load a backing track and export both WAV audio and a visualizer video.
A DAW plugin beta using the same speech synthesis engines has also been announced, with a crossgrade purchase option attached.

A “classic” version, stripped of the piano roll, polyphony and extra voice engines, runs free in the browser. The Android version is free on Google Play with a one-time payment to unlock Pro, and a DRM-free bundle covering Windows, macOS, Linux and Android costs $9.99 on itch.io.
Scaler Music has unveiled Scaler EQ Pro. It's a major expansion of the note-aware EQ, which boosts or cuts frequencies based on whether they belong to the song's key and scale.
The core is technology covered by US patent 12,647,085. Key detection runs automatically, so changing the key or scale never means redrawing the EQ curve from scratch.
Filter slopes move continuously instead of snapping between fixed steps. Musical bands now sit alongside traditional band types, and tilt, notch and magic shelf have been newly added.

The most unfamiliar part of this release is Live Mode. You play which frequencies to boost or cut using a MIDI keyboard or MIDI recorded in a DAW. Velocity is recognized, and ADSR lets the response change over time. Performance Solo follows the playing directly, while Live Band Solo isolates just the band being touched right now.

Dedicated bass and treble compressors have been added. Dynamic EQ with threshold, ratio, attack and release runs on every band, and sidechain input lets an external signal drive individual bands. Continuous gain match keeps correcting for level changes, so it's less likely you'll mistake something getting louder for something sounding better.

Mid/side can be applied per band, with stereo width and low-end mono control included. Input and output meters show peak and RMS, and peak limiters sit at both ends of the signal. Processing is minimum phase with zero latency, so it works for mixing and tracking as well as on a live stage.

It runs as 64-bit VST3, AU and AAX on macOS 12 and above, and as VST3 and AAX on Windows 10 and above. A standalone version is included as well. It's priced at $99 and launches September 23. Buying Scaler EQ now for $59 gets a free upgrade to Pro at launch.
Sonos CEO Tom Conrad explained how custom agents work. It's a feature that lets listeners build their own AI assistant within the Sonos ecosystem.
Here's Conrad in his own words: “An Anthropic engine, an OpenAI engine, a Gemini engine, a Grok engine — you can pick whichever reasoning engine you want and summon it within Sonos.”

After picking one, you choose a voice, give it a name and build a personality. The example Conrad gave was the John Cusack character from the movie “High Fidelity.” It's a picture of a record-store obsessive with strong opinions living inside the speaker, recommending music and quietly coloring the listener's point of view.

You can run several agents at once. Music recommendations might run on OpenAI, cooking advice on Anthropic, and finding nearby live shows on yet another one. Each has its own separate personality and purpose.

This extends a trend in which Sonos has been opening its devices up to multiple AI assistants and third parties. Voice control is moving from a window that takes dictated commands toward something more like a companion with its own taste.

blocks.cap: Sung Cho, Chartmetric founder and CEO

blocks.x: Music data analytics company Chartmetric released Flow, an AI agent meant to expand and simplify subscribers' working tools.

In the words of Chartmetric founder and CEO Sung Cho, Flow is definitely not “just another AI chatbot.” According to the company, it unpacks complex analysis and identifies how, why and where audiences respond to a given artist.
It also builds weekly reports for flagship releases, drafts multi-phase marketing plans, and tracks millions of tracks across major services.

“Flow is a new product built for people working in the music industry, riding on the solid data pipeline Chartmetric has built over the last 10 years,” Cho said. “It thinks through the best strategy from a music industry perspective, and cross-references your data against 14 million artists.”
Flow layers Chartmetric's own datasets and proprietary technology on top of existing AI models. It scans through trillions of data points and returns analysis and recommendations in near real time.

Akash Mukherjee, Chartmetric's chief product officer, said, “We've been building Flow for two years and plan to keep refining it going forward. Flow is a member of the team. It handles tasks, sets schedules, automates things, and works as a partner thinking alongside you in the background.”

Premium subscribers at $150 a month use Flow Lite. The $180-a-month Ultra package includes the full feature set, and the standalone subscription is $60 a month. Credits run 20 a month for Premium and 100 a month for Ultra and the standalone subscription, with extras available for purchase if needed.

Cho said “more than 4,000 users have used the Flow app to answer questions that used to take an entire research session.” Those include things like who an artist's audience actually is, what drove a spike or a drop, and how they stack up against peers across every platform. “The story you used to piece together by hand, bouncing between charts, filters and spreadsheets, now comes back from a single conversation, ready to save, export and act on. Moving from tracking what happened to understanding why it happened and deciding what to do next — that's the shift Flow creates.”

A seven-day trial comes with every dashboard tier. During the trial, Flow credits are capped at 10, after which the monthly allotment opens up. Chartmetric was among the first in the music data industry to open an MCP server earlier this year, and MCP access is now included in every subscription plan.

blocks.cap: Jason Isbell on the exhibit stage at the Country Music Hall of Fame, November 2025

blocks.x: Jason Isbell is leading a new class action lawsuit against Suno, claiming the company designed its AI music generator to call up artists' identifiable traits.

Filed on Monday, August 31, and obtained by Billboard, the complaint argues that Suno embedded musicians' entire musical personas into its model as tokens, violating what's known as the right of publicity. As a result, the complaint says, a user can type in just a musician's name and get songs, descriptions and artwork that “evoke the identity of a beloved musician.”

The complaint puts it this way: “The Suno system recognizes 'Jason Isbell' as something far larger than a mere string of characters. The name functions as a search key that pulls up a bundle of performer-specific representations, and the system uses it to generate responses tied to that musician.” In other words, entering just a name brings back songs, descriptive attributes and related imagery associated with that musician all at once.
As an example, the complaint cites entering Isbell's name producing an Americana song called “Paper Bell,” a result that mimicked Isbell's distinctively clear male vocals and country-style vibrato.

Joining Isbell as plaintiffs are David Lowery, frontman of Camper Van Beethoven and a longtime artist rights advocate, blues singer Guy Forsyth, and jazz saxophonist Ed Calle. Their goal is to represent, as a class, every musician whose name has been accepted as a Suno prompt.

Suno has said it uses filters to block prompts naming specific artists. The complaint says those filters frequently don't work, and that even when they do, they're “easily defeated” by putting spaces between the letters of a name. Entering “m i c h a e l j a c k s o n” produced a pop song called “Glovebox Moonwalk” that even came with Michael Jackson's signature white-glove imagery; “t a y l o r s w i f t” produced a Taylor Swift-style breakup song; and “b a d b u n n y” produced a Bad Bunny-style Spanish-language reggaeton track.

Isbell's side alleges violations of right-of-publicity statutes in states including New York, California and Tennessee. Since that right is separate from copyright, the argument goes, an artist can bring their own claim over their name even if their label has already licensed music to Suno. Warner Music Group licensed with Suno last fall, and BMG did so last month. The suit seeks unspecified damages and argues the class of plaintiffs could run into the “millions.”

A Suno spokesperson told Billboard on September 1 that “we believe this claim is without merit and intend to defend against it.” “Suno isn't in the business of selling anyone's name — it's a place that helps people make new, original music. We stand behind the numerous safeguards we've built across the platform, including blocking prompts for specific artist names or copyrighted songs.”
Soundboost added engine v4 to its browser mastering service. Instead of building a mastering chain from scratch, you can just write out what you want in plain language.
The workflow is simple: upload your mix, describe the result you want, and compare the master Soundboost produces against the original.
You might ask for something warmer or louder without crushing the dynamics. If you don't like the result, there's no need to start over — just refine it with another request.
The final call is still yours. A built-in A/B comparison makes it easier to decide which master to pick.
Soundboost works more like an assistant for the finishing stage. That's especially true when you need a starting point for mastering, or want to test several directions before committing to one.

There are six starting profiles: Balanced, Warm, Punch, Loud, Clear and Vintage. You can also search for a reference track, tweak the final EQ by hand, compare revisions, and carry a master's seed number over to another track to match the tone across an EP or a whole album.

Engine v4 is a ground-up rewrite of the processing behind the service. Soundboost says it's about 35 percent faster, mastering a 3-minute song in just over 10 seconds. Every master coming out of the platform now runs on this engine.

Because it runs in the browser, there's no plugin or desktop installer to deal with. The same account also works in the iOS and Android apps, so you can switch to a phone or tablet whenever that's more convenient.
Free previews work without creating an account. There's also a free mode for full exports, though the current version inserts a random vocal tag into the finished file.
A free stem separation feature is also available without registration. It splits a track into five parts you can adjust for level, pan, mute, solo, loop, pitch and tempo in the browser mixer.

The Unlimited plan, at $16 a month or $48 a year, gives unlimited masters, WAV export, effects and 15 revisions per track. Unlimited Plus, at $24 a month or $72 a year, adds bulk mastering, unlimited revisions, extra stems and drum separation.

blocks.cap: BMG, which licensed with Suno last month

Believe becomes the latest company to work with Suno, following BMG and Warner Music Group. Acon Digital has released Acoustica 8, a version that reworks the interface, adds support for immersive formats, and brings AI restoration features.

Acoustica first launched in 2002. It began as a cheaper alternative to editors like Sound Forge or WaveLab, and over the years grew into a DAW that covers post-production, audio restoration, spectral editing and multichannel surround.
The redrawn interface adds docking windows, letting users build their own workflow from the processing modules they use most. A new start screen also jumps straight into recent projects.

blocks.cap: Acoustica 8 · Source: Acon Digital

It's long-awaited news. Audacity, the open-source audio editor owned by MuseGroup, has reached version 4, with a redesigned interface and refined usability. There's also a fork worth watching.

Audacity passed 100 million cumulative downloads in a bit over 25 years. It started as a community-driven project, but its owner today is MuseGroup, the company behind MuseScore notation software and publishing giant Hal Leonard. Even so, Audacity remains free and open source under the GPLv3.

The core of this release is the new interface, the most noticeable set of changes in the software's 26-year history. An outdated UI and inconsistent editing behavior had long held the software back, which stung more given its role as a first stop for beginners looking for free audio tools on Mac, Windows and Linux.

Among the additions: a split tool, free clip placement, multi-clip select/move/trim/stretch, clip groups, gain envelopes, trim/stretch handles, markers and regions, multiple workspaces, a completely redrawn effects UI, the MuseHub effects marketplace, LV2/VST3/AU support, and compatibility with Audacity 3's aup3 files. The price remains free forever under the GPLv3.

MuseGroup would probably like to push talk of ecosystems and cloud sharing, but plenty of people dislike that kind of extra baggage. This release makes all of it easy to skip. Right below the “recommended” MuseHub version on the download page sits a plain application bundle. It doesn't even need an internet connection to install, so it can be handed out on a USB drive at a workshop. No features are missing — things like effects can simply be added later.

blocks.cap: Audacity 4's new interface

blocks.x: The Audacity 4 UI that results is minimal and very clean. It's also fast — it's built with Qt — and feels just as comfortable as other paid software.

blocks.cap: The new spectral view

blocks.x: The spectral view is good too. Built-in effects that used to have thin UIs have been redrawn for a modern look. Some of what MuseGroup has added is worth a look too. The new plugin marketplace has quite a few decent free plugins for everything from music to podcasts, and since it's opt-in, nothing feels forced. From this point on, though, you're outside open source.

Audacity isn't as deep as the free DAW Ardour — they're different tools. If Ardour is a true DAW, Audacity is a true wave editor. The toolset built up from 25 years of community work is still there, and thanks to the improved editing, switching over from Ardour doesn't feel unfamiliar. The plugin scanner repeatedly crashing on Mac is a snag. Dismissing the dialog let most plugins work normally.

blocks.cap: The fork project Tenacity

blocks.x: There's also the fork story. Since the acquisition, there's been wariness toward MuseGroup from the community and the open-source camp. Being GPLv3 means it stays free forever, but free software isn't only about license and price. When a large company steps in, the center of gravity for responsibility and control shifts.

That's what led to Tenacity. It's a project that several fork attempts merged into, with plenty of work put into usability and features too. Like Audacity, it's scriptable and accessible, but it's completely FLOSS with no proprietary bundling at all. It runs on Apple silicon, Intel and ARM, and Mac binaries are back. It's also on MacPorts.
In the end, it's the same core. Whether Tenacity adopts Audacity 4's UI changes remains to be seen. Either way, there's excellent free software here.

The headline feature for this version is Lucid Beatgrid, a major overhaul of beat-detection technology. Serato describes it as “the most accurate and intuitive beatgrid technology we've ever built.”

The new beat grid changes the analysis method itself, so it tracks songs with fluctuating BPM more closely. Playing back old funk, soul and disco records cut without a click track or DAW timeline now needs fewer manual fixes and plays back more steadily.

blocks.cap: Serato 5.0 also reworked its beat grid editing tools (Image credit: Serato)

Another major change is streaming service integration. As before, mixing tracks from Apple Music, Tidal, Beatport, SoundCloud and Spotify inside Serato DJ only requires the relevant subscription. What's new is mixing tracks from different platforms together with your own library in one place, without having to log in and out of accounts.

In the library, each streaming service now shows up as its own crate. A new provider search dropdown makes it easier to find tracks across multiple services, and streaming tracks now show BPM and key before analysis, so you can pick and prep them on the spot.

blocks.cap: Cue loops are new to Serato DJ Pro (Image credit: Serato)

blocks.x: Both features come to Serato DJ Pro and the free Serato DJ Lite alike. Pro users also get one more addition: cue loops. These save a loop as a cue point, letting you jump straight to that spot and trigger it instantly whenever you need it.
Serato 5.0 is in public beta now. More details are on Serato's blog, The Drop, which is also where you sign up to join the beta.

blocks.x: AI music platform Suno unveiled a new family of music generation models. It's the first one developed in partnership with major labels after signing licensing deals with Warner Music Group and BMG.

The company calls V6 the best it has ever built. It describes it as “faster, more expressive and higher quality,” with new tools for precisely steering output. Having learned “more of the language and building blocks musicians use,” prompts can now include vocals and instrumentation, structure, mood or feel, and even references outside of music.

V6 launches in three versions. The flagship V6, for Pro and Premium subscribers, reliably delivers “polished music across every genre and style.” V6-wild, available only to paid subscribers, is built for experimentation and aims for “unexpected textures and ambition.” The one model open to all users is the fast, lightweight V6-mini.

Control is also finer-grained than in previous generations. Prompts can edit a specific part of an existing song, combine elements from multiple songs, or pull an element out of one track and build something new on top of it. Beyond text and audio, images and video can now also serve as a starting point for a track.

With V6's launch, all of Suno's previous models are permanently retired. The company says the old models were trained on tens of millions of songs, including copyrighted ones, but V6 was trained from scratch. The training data doesn't overlap with before, either — it blends licensed data secured through industry partnerships with user data, including licensed recordings from the Warner Music Group and BMG catalogs.

blocks.cap: (Image credit: Suno)

blocks.x: Warner and BMG said artists and songwriters will be compensated under the partnership. Neither company disclosed how much individual creators receive or how the money is split.

The same day, Suno also announced a partnership with Believe, a company that provides distribution, publishing and artist development to independent musicians and labels, and the owner of TuneCore. Tracks made with Suno will be distributed through Believe and TuneCore, and music from participating Believe and TuneCore artists and labels will be used to train V6. Believe said “artists who opt in will be compensated for their music and have their rights protected.”

A new product that lets individual artists co-create and remix their own music is also in development. Participating artists will be compensated, and Suno claims the product “opens revenue opportunities across the music ecosystem.”

The shift toward licensed data comes against a backdrop of legal disputes with the industry. Warner Music Group settled a copyright lawsuit last year and struck the partnership that led to V6's development, but Universal Music Group and Sony Music continue their lawsuits, alleging infringement on a “almost unimaginable scale.” Suno maintains its use is fair use. In a press release, CEO Shulman said the launch of V6 is “the start of a new chapter for music.”

blocks.x: Universal Music Group has signed a multi-year licensing agreement with AI audio company ElevenLabs. According to a press release, the two companies will build an AI music platform for fans “built on licensed music and artist participation,” and will also co-develop AI audio products for artists and songwriters.

On the platform, fans will co-create, remix and mash up music from artists and songwriters who opt in. Layering on the AI voice replication ElevenLabs has been known for, it will also produce “personalized vocal experiences.” The release added that the companies will “develop additional products and fan experiences over the coming months and years.”

The weight of this deal falls on co-developing new products rather than on ElevenLabs' existing music services. Both ElevenMusic, its music generation and editing app, and Music EPI, its studio-grade music model offered via API, are outside the scope of the deal.

The news comes exactly one day after Suno, the biggest name in generative AI music, released v6, its first family of models built “in partnership with the music industry.” In a Billboard On the Record interview, Suno CEO Mikey Shulman said v6 was trained on music provided by WMG, Believe and BMG — UMG's rivals — and on platform “user interactions.” Universal, together with Sony Music, continues its lawsuit against Suno, alleging widespread copyright infringement.

ElevenLabs has already struck several deals with the music industry, including with Merlin, the digital licensing body representing 30,000 independent labels and distributors, and Kobalt, a major independent publisher. Its earliest known partnership was with the production music library SoundAudio, announced in 2025.

Universal Music Group Chairman and CEO Lucian Grainge described the deal this way: “The most exciting possibilities in AI and music come from putting artists, songwriters and fans at the center. UMG and ElevenLabs share the view that responsible AI can spark discovery, deepen the relationship between artists and fans, and open new revenue opportunities for the creative community.”

ElevenLabs co-founder and CEO Mati Staniszewski also said, “AI opens up incredible possibilities for the music and artists we love,” adding, “By combining our models and products with UMG's global community and rights management capabilities, we'll help artists and songwriters build new experiences for fans and be fairly compensated.”

The music industry's conversation around AI has focused on consent, disclosure, and labeling. For independent artists, that's only the starting line, writes Michael T. Neely, president of the Global Music Conference. When a dispute actually breaks out, what decides it isn't whether something felt unauthorized, but whether you can prove what was agreed, what was produced, what changed, who held the files, and where the money moved. Major labels have legal teams, rights management systems, and internal audit trails. Independent artists are left with a few texts, scattered emails, cloud folders, and verbal agreements.

That's why there are five records worth keeping. The first is a document spelling out the scope of consent. The word “permission” alone is too vague. The document should state exactly how far someone was allowed to use vocals, likeness, compositions, stems, and datasets — for a single song or a whole campaign, for model training, exclusively or with the right to sublicense, and whether a synthetic voice can be made and used in advertising. Keep the signed copy, the platform terms in effect at the time, any later revisions, and records of any time permissions were changed or withdrawn.

The second is provenance records. Keep original vocal takes, multitrack sessions, stems, project files, lyrics, and dated demos not as backups but as evidence of where the work came from and how it grew. C2PA's Content Credentials have already set a standard for this, but it's enough to follow the basic principle: don't overwrite originals, and preserve dated versions and metadata.

The third is version history. AI can produce dozens or hundreds of outputs at once. Logging each step — whether lyrics were revised, backing vocals were synthesized, or instruments were swapped — separates what a person made from what AI added, and what was approved from what was never cleared for release. This connects directly to the Copyright Office's continued emphasis on human authorship.

The fourth is a record of earnings and use: settlement statements, distributor reports, platform dashboards, licensing invoices, sync payments, neighboring-rights settlements, and distribution breakdowns. Dashboards change later, so download them periodically. The fifth is a record of disputes and corrections: the initial complaint, takedown requests, ticket numbers, communications with distributors and labels, screenshots of the disputed content, response dates, the outcome of any dispute, and any settlement or correction. The advice adds one more thing: don't let an important conversation end with just a phone call — follow up with a brief confirmation email.

blocks.cap: Initial Audio Difro Melody AI

blocks.x: Initial Audio has released Difro Melody AI, a standalone MIDI generator for macOS and Windows, and it's free. It runs inference locally on the CPU, or on the GPU if one is available, with no cloud involved.

It doesn't compose a song from a blank screen. Feed it a MIDI file you made, and it reads the rhythm, melodic contour, and chord progression to produce variations that keep the character of the original idea. The architecture pairs a Variational Autoencoder with a Transformer. You can drag in a MIDI file or play directly into the piano roll. Results can be dragged into a DAW or exported as WAV.

The free tier includes 10 prompt models, around 80 SourceLab Light presets, and VST3/AU plugin hosting. Generation, though, is capped at 50 times a month. Removing that cap and being able to build your own prompt models requires Pro, at $49.

Initial Audio describes Difro as a personal AI co-producer. The company says it isn't a tool that scatters notes at random, but one that analyzes the MIDI a user hands it, using that as its reference point.

blocks.cap: Positive Grid Spark Pedal

blocks.x: Positive Grid's Spark amp opened a path for carrying amp and effects modeling onto the stage, becoming the lineup's most popular line. The new Spark Pedal, which inherits that name, packs the same platform into a stompbox.

It runs the same HD Tone Engine that powers the flagship Spark 2, and includes 33 amp models and 43 effects. You can browse more than 100,000 tones from the ToneCloud community, and it loads presets saved on other Spark-series products as is. Practice quietly through headphone output, or play along with your favorite songs over Bluetooth. It also runs on battery power, so placement isn't an issue.

A multifunction knob on top controls both the amp and effects. In Amp mode, it adjusts Gain, Bass, Mid, and Treble; in FX mode, it adjusts Drive, modulation, delay, and reverb. Holding down the center knob turns on the built-in tuner. The footswitch handles recording, overdubbing, and undo for the 60-second looper, and the same switch saves six presets across two banks.

The free companion app handles the rest. Type a phrase, a song, an artist, or a feeling into Text to Tone, and it recommends a matching tone, which you can then refine or save. Build Your Rig lets you build a signal chain from the amp, cabinet, and effects library and adjust the details. Auto Chords displays guitar chords in real time while a song plays through the app. The pedal's looper can also be controlled remotely from the app.
The Spark Pedal is already on sale, priced at $199.

blocks.cap: The Tone3000 plugin handles NAM A2 captures both as a standalone app and inside a DAW. (Image credit: Tone3000)

blocks.x: Tone3000 has quietly changed how guitarists find their sound. Built on open-source Neural Amp Modeler technology, it's home to the world's largest collection of community-made NAM A2 captures and IRs. Capture your own analog gear — a tube amp, an overdrive pedal, a fuzz, whatever it is — upload it, and anyone can use it. Hardware like Blackstar and HeadRush has started supporting Tone3000 natively.

Now that library opens directly inside a free, open-source plugin that runs both in a DAW and as a standalone app. Chains is the core feature: it links together user-made NAM A2 captures and IRs to build an entire signal path. You might put an EP-3 boost in front of a slightly pushed Marshall JCM800 capture, stack on a Keeley Mk3 Driver for extra grit if you feel like it, and finish with whichever IR you want.

There's no limit to how many you stack. You can run two chains at once split left and right for stereo work, and Spread widens a mono signal without splitting it into stereo. There's a global EQ across the whole chain plus separate pre- and post-parametric EQ per block. Finer settings like oversampling, MIDI mapping, and per-block normalization are included too.

The ultimate goal is a simpler workflow. There's no need for a third-party NAM player, and anything uploaded to the library opens inside the plugin the moment it goes up. You manage and organize favorites and drop them into your existing in-the-box setup. Tone3000 co-founder and CEO Stanley Vergilis said that because it's open source, this is the worst it will ever be, and he's looking forward to seeing what the community builds.

Apple held a product event last night. New iPhones, including a folding model, along with AirPods and Apple Watch took the stage. But the announcement that stood out most on the music side was something else: 'Audio Intelligence.'

blocks.cap: Song info displayed on Apple Watch

blocks.x: What is it, and why does it matter? It's a feature built into the new Apple Watch hardware and software, described as using AI to “detect sounds, identify music, and help you stay present, while protecting your privacy at every step.”
In short, if you're wearing an Apple Watch, the watch keeps listening to its surroundings through the microphone. It's not far off from what a smart speaker does.

It alerts you when a doorbell or alarm goes off, a feature useful for people with hearing loss. It also takes “notes” on conversations throughout the day to create a summary you can read later, and 'Live Rewind' lets you open a record of what was said in the previous 15 seconds.

And then there's Shazam. Apple wrote in its summary that “Shazam music recognition automatically detects the song playing in the background, surfacing the title and artist name in the Smart Stack without even tapping the widget.”
Automatic Shazam tagging itself isn't new; it's been in the mobile app for well over a decade. But moving it onto people's wrists is a new development.

A watch that listens all day raises privacy concerns, both for the wearer and for people nearby, and around how Apple stores and uses that data. Apple is sensitive to this, too, and issued a separate 'Privacy Overview' document addressing each point.
Denon DJ has released Prime 4 G2, the latest in its all-in-one DJ system line. It's a 4-channel unit that pulls in a few interesting features Akai recently added to its MPC line.

Prime 4 G2 is fully standalone, running on its own built-in CPU. You can mix from music stored on its onboard storage or stream over Wi-Fi. A structure it calls 'omnisource' lets it move smoothly between standalone DJing and acting as a controller for software like Serato DJ Pro and Algoriddim djay.

blocks.cap: Denon DJ Prime 4 G2

blocks.x: Moving to this second generation, Denon looked to Akai Pro, a fellow member of the inMusic family. It carried over much of what's been improved in the recent MPC line, and the most eye-catching of those is the multi-expression MPCe pad found on the MPC Live III and MPC XL.

The MPCe pad reads velocity and pressure together and is split into four zones along the X/Y axes, which means each of the 16 pads can run multiple functions. You can trigger multiple hot cues or samples, manipulate stems, apply rolls, play effects, and even control lighting.

blocks.cap: The top panel with MPCe pads

blocks.x: How useful this multi-expression control turns out to be in the booth depends on how much of a 'performance' DJ you are. Stacking that many functions onto 16 pads could be overkill for many users. A quick-handed, performance-oriented DJ will likely find fun new ways to expand a set with it.

Like the MPC, the G2 got a major internal upgrade. It carries an 8-core ARM processor and 4GB of RAM, which Denon says amounts to four times the processing power of the previous generation. Finding and loading tracks is faster now.

More importantly, the unit can render and manipulate track stems on its own in standalone mode. The effects list has also grown, with more than 25 Main FX, 10 Touch FX, four Fader FX, and four Sweep FX.

blocks.cap: Prime 4 G2

blocks.x: As with its predecessor, a 10.1-inch touchscreen remains the center of software control. The jog wheel grew from 6 inches to 8 inches, and the dual-rail faders were redesigned.
With a subscription, you can stream wirelessly from Amazon Music Unlimited, Apple Music, Beatport, SoundCloud Go+, and TIDAL. Bluetooth for pairing tablets and smartphones is included as well.

A 3-pin DMX output lets you control lighting directly without a separate interface. A Zone output, which sends a fully independent signal apart from the main output, also lets event or party DJs play music in two rooms at once.

Jason Stout, product manager for inMusic's DJ brands, said “performance-focused DJs want the technology to fade into the background so creativity can stand center stage.” “As someone who DJs frequently at upscale events, I rely on gear that adapts as fast as the crowd does. Prime 4 G2 brings together powerful performance tools, onboard Stems, streaming access, and integrated DMX lighting control in a single workflow, letting DJs shape both the music and the mood without missing a beat.”
Prime 4 G2 is available now, priced at $2,599 USD / €2,699.99 / £2,299.99.

Sean Parker, the Napster co-founder, has jumped back into the music industry, and he tells The Information that he's playing by the rules this time. (Asking for forgiveness rather than permission didn't work out so well last time around, he readily concedes.)

Two years ago, he joined an $80 million rescue of Stability AI, the image-generator startup that nearly collapsed after overspending and internal turmoil led to founder Emad Mostaque's ouster. Now Parker and his longtime friend Prem Akkaraju, who became CEO, are taking the wraps off what they've been building.

The big idea, Parker says, is to turn Stability into the go-to AI toolmaker for music professionals. Toward that end, in late August, the company announced $76 million in funding from, among others, Sony, Warner, and Universal, which also licensed their catalogs for training as part of the deal. Stability has since released three new audio models and AI music-editing software. The AI can generate whole instrumental tracks or short snippets from text prompts. Parker says an upcoming update will let users hum a melody or beatbox a drum pattern to steer it.

On Billboard On the Record, Questlove traces sampling from the Fairlight and Marley Marl to Public Enemy's It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back, his 1988 "Eureka moment," and asks how microchopping, catalog sales and generative AI may pose new opportunities or risks to the art form.
"Between 1988 and 1991, it was the Wild West. No one was policing us," he says, until the Biz Markie lawsuit made permission the rule.
"There's always a debate about AI versus making something yourself — microwaving versus cooking a full meal. To me, there has always been magic in imperfection."
Sonically he is "not there yet" on AI music because of its digital distortion, though models may perfect it in ten years. "But I see AI as a parallel to sampling culture."
"If you're building an AI system, you should be transparent about the material used to build the platform, and there should be compensation for it."

In an op-ed, LyricFind founder and CEO Darryl Ballantyne argues that while generative AI needs licensing, transparency and guardrails, AI in lyrics, rights data and metadata can help existing works earn more.

Lyric royalties are usage-driven, so gaps in availability mean fewer displays and less money for rightsholders. Manual transcription, sync and translation set a break-even point that limited how deep into the catalogue the industry could go.

Per Luminate, 9.6M songs were streamed 10,000 to 500,000 times in 2025, over 13% of global stream volume. LyricFind uses AI for first-pass transcription, then word-by-word sync and translation, with humans verifying throughout.

Making staff three or four times more efficient grows viable content by about 700%, he says, so it makes sense to double the human team. Even a 99% accurate system on 100 million lyrics would leave a million errors.
Go behind the scenes with Braylon Browner and Emmy award winning choreographer/director Nina McNeely to see what it takes to go from dance, to song, to complete creative world built around movement.

"It's amazing to be able to edit the music as you go," Browner says, so that dance and music "really meet together and work perfectly in harmony." McNeely adds that Suno "is giving the choreographers the power back to change the song to match our choreographic ideas."

Suno is now “far beyond” the 2 million paid subscribers and USD $300 million in revenue it last disclosed, co-founder and CEO Mikey Shulman said at Bloomberg's Screentime conference on October 1. He did not put a new number on either figure.

Asked what Warner Music Group and BMG are paying Suno for, Shulman said: “Imagine, you can take the music of one of your favorite artists and start to play with it and remix it or cover it or mash it up with something else… This is an entirely new product.”

Suno settled WMG's lawsuit in November 2025, signed BMG on August 12 and Believe on September 8, and launched its v6 models with those partners on September 9. Universal and Sony sued again on September 18.
On labelling AI music, Shulman said no single party should decide, and “it's actually good that we don't have firm rules of the road just yet.”
What happens when music students bring Suno into their creative process?

In this episode of In The Cut, we visit Seoul Institute of the Arts in Seoul, South Korea to see how students are using Suno to develop ideas, experiment with vocals and harmonies, find chords, create sounds they might not otherwise be able to record, and bring those ideas into their existing production workflows.

From generating the starting point of a song to separating stems in Suno Studio and continuing the work inside a DAW, the students share how Suno can help them move faster while still shaping the final music themselves.

The North Carolina man who used artificial intelligence to create thousands of fake songs by invented artists, then unleashed an army of bot accounts to stream the tracks billions of times, should face “significant punishment,” prosecutors say.

Manhattan federal prosecutors urged a judge to sentence Michael Smith to at least 46 months behind bars. Smith's defense is asking for probation only; federal probation officials recommend 24 months. Sentencing is set for Oct. 6.

In April 2023, Taylor Swift's entire catalog drew 9.3 million streams from YouTube Music family-plan subscribers, prosecutors said, while Smith's generated 80.9 million. They said he pocketed more than $8 million in unearned royalties over more than six years.

Smith pleaded guilty in March to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and agreed to pay $8,091,843.64 in forfeiture. His lawyers said he was “profoundly sorry” but “did not set out to commit a federal crime.”

Suno is branching out from AI music with Speech, a feature that generates spoken voices from scripts or prompted descriptions. It is now in public beta on Suno's web and mobile platforms, and generates voiceovers together with background music to accompany them.
Chief product officer Jack Brody called it "the first audio model that generates voice and music together as one cohesive track," adding that music "will always be at the heart of Suno."

AI speech is hardly new: DeepMind, Adobe and ElevenLabs, one of the most recognizable platforms since 2023, are already there. The Verge suggests Suno is likely trying to diversify a platform whose music generator has drawn many lawsuits.

The music is optional and can be toggled off for clean speech. In the Create tab, Simple mode takes a prompt such as "a pirate captain rallying his crew," while Advanced mode accepts a custom script and adjusts voice gender, speech style and variety. Clips run up to about eight minutes.
"Beta really does mean beta," Brody said. "Occasionally, British accents can wander off to Australia and back."
